Scanning errors corrected: 'nammae' read as 'flammae' (1.13); 'Darn postmodum regnatons' as 'Darii postmodum regnantis' (1.19); stray 'i' before 'Ezechiae' omitted (1.15); 'am-10 monuit' as 'ammonuit' (1.27); 'lignee' taken as vocative 'ligneus', 'wooden man' (1.26). 1.14: the wordplay links Greek Ἠλίας (Elijah) with ἥλιος (sun). 1.17 'imagineum supplicium': taken as the punishment for refusing the image. 1.20 final sentence is syntactically loose; the dative 'conditori' is construed with 'subiacent'. 1.27: the quotation is Lucan, Pharsalia 7 (dialogue form); 'paliurus' rendered as Christ's-thorn.

nodes.text: THE PREFACE OF SEDULIUS'S PASCHAL WORK.

Whoever you are, guest, who share in the Paschal feast, and have not disdained to recline on our couches: lay aside the raised height of your brow, if you come as a dear friend, and do not look here for the work of a skilled book, but gladly accept the slight ceremonies of a small table, take them up contentedly, and be glad to be filled in mind rather than with food. Or if you are rather taken with a great abundance of rich things and, fond of luxury, expect exceptional riches, you ought to be sated at the dinners of noble learned men, whose manifold provisions cannot be recounted. There you will surely find whatever edible thing the wave of the sea nourishes, whatever the fruitfulness of the earth supplies, whatever holds its body up among the clouds by the balance of its wings. On the very dishes, too, studded with jewels in a variety all too costly, honey turns golden with its nectar-sweet combs, and the honeycomb, set out in golden baskets, plays in colour against the metal. But we have plucked cheap greens from the seeds of a poor man's garden, which we are seen to serve in a red earthenware dish with goodwill rather than with splendour.
BOOK ONE.

Since the studious habit of the pagan poets commends the trifles of fabulous song with the pomp of noble words, and, whether with the shouts of buskined tragedy, or the comic foulness of laughable Geta, or with any measures of the metrical art, they hand down the criminal deeds of ancient times, and some things too composed with the art of shameful narration, as the reed ploughs across the papyrus of the Nile's flood: why should I, who, practising on the ten-stringed psaltery the songs of David's melody among the choirs of the blessed teaching, answer reverently with spiritual words, keep silent with suppressed voice about the wonderful and saving mighty works of Christ, when I ought to take up the work of truth and not be silent, with the instrument of faithful speech, about the gifts of heavenly grace? For the service of the human heart and mind attends on no one more justly than on the almighty Lord, who established the senses and founded hearts, so that matter ever devoted to its Creator should not abandon its own maker, from whom it is fitting that a work of his own right be neither withdrawn nor lost; who in perpetual dominion in the citadels of heaven has one power with the Father, equal brightness of splendour, the undivided sublimity of a shared summit, equal honour, the same might, a shared height, a kingdom infinite in time, a beginning ever abiding in unbroken eternity, a glory partnered in the sharing of the sceptre, and a like majesty. This is the way leading to the dwelling of salvation; this is the path opened to firm steps toward the Paschal gifts. Here we shall lay the foundations of our work; here, then, all of you, turn your sick minds; apply this medicine to your deadly diseases, you whom the vain purpose of harmful disputation creeps upon, and whom the incurable discipline of Attic teaching wounds with the poison of Cecropian doctrine, so that, when you breathe in the life-giving airs, the breaths of the divine law, the scent of grace fragrant with sweetness, you may thereafter with purer mind leave behind the gluttony of Athenian filth. Why, sons of Theseus, do you go round the labyrinthine windings in dark wanderings, and, your tracks entangled with the exit lost, roam the gloomy caves in blind mazes? Why do you still prefer the wild vine to the good vine? Why do you place the little willow before the gleaming rose-beds? Why trust with empty worship in stone images and bronze figures, or what will it profit to condemn souls to slavery to profane shrines and venerated metals? Spare, I beg, spare at last [to work] the rough clods of sandy dust and to enjoy the bare dryness of barren fields, where the plough-lands, never with pregnant womb, have known how to relieve the toil of the sweating farmer with fruitful reward. Do not pluck from the shoots of the bloody turf the poisonous nourishment of deadly juice, which, ever friendly to the foods of Tartarus, do not know how to serve life, but death. Rather, enter the pleasant meadows of flowering grass and the lovely approaches of the blessed seat through the clear waters of the pure spring, where the fruitfulness of life-giving seeds, quickened by divine waters, nourishes a crop, the roughness of growing thorns torn out, which by the great abundance of manifold fruit can now be God's harvest and, opening the hope of future reward, may store its fruit in hundredfold heaps in the greatest granaries.

Almighty God of undivided and eternal godhead, who hold the whole world by your holy nod, who made firm the structure of heaven by the work of your fingers and founded its fabric by your mighty word, who by fixed bounds forbid the raging madness of the surging sea to overwhelm the border of the neighbouring land, who, setting the face of the radiant sun and the horned countenance of the moon alongside day and night, dispense the alternations of both lights in the holy balance of your governance, who alone gather and alone know the number of the stars, their powers, signs, names, places, courses and times; who animated the sluggish limbs of the raw earth with living bodies in diverse motions; who, after you condemn to death the man eating the fruits of the tree in forbidden presumption, raise him up again by the sacrament of a better food, and preserve him from the pleasurable deceit of the viper's bite by the drink of spotless blood; who, when the name of the human race, apart from those whom the ark had protected as a guardian, was wholly drowned and buried by the sudden flood of the rising deluge, restored and multiplied it again from one stock, so that by the demonstration of a mystical power you might reveal that what the sins of the flesh had slain, walled by the faithful protection of wood, was to be washed through the one baptism of the whole world: graciously show me now, your suppliant, that way, that path, which directs the steps of the few by a narrow track to the walls of the saving city, namely Jerusalem, the Lord's city, which bears our Passover in the passion of Christ, so that through this city, which performs the hospitality of bodily grace, we may deserve to reach that homeland of spiritual glory; and let your word, Lord, be a lamp to my feet, by which the brightness of the right road may lead me to those places of flowering grass where the good shepherd keeps his shining fold, where the whole white-robed flock follows the Lamb of the virgin ewe, most pure in snowy brightness. The way is not difficult, if you deign to offer yourself as guide. All things lie under your power, all nature yields to your commands and passes into contrary forms and shapes at your sovereign order. If you will that the yearly crops turn golden in icy seasons, sluggish winter brings out the nimble reaper with sickles; if, in the mild weather of the spring region, when the earth shines covered with the first mantle of flowers, you bid the vine bring forth with laden shoots, the vintner, dancing in a river of must, will drive out the nectar-sweet innards of the happy grape with the welcome injury of the drunken heel: and the alternations of all seasons, their fruits changed, will not refuse to serve the Creator. For hoary faith reveals evidence of divine wonders, and the ancient origin of the old fathers is witness, and the immortal signs of heavenly powers endure, not to be abolished though ages pass and time grows old. Of these, with the fear of a trembling mind, we scarcely permit our spirits and feeble heart to touch on at least a few in bold narration, so that, entering a forest of great density, I may strive to reach some branches with the very tips of my fingers. For even if a hundred mouths at once were supplied to a human body, and an iron voice did not cease to cry out with a hundred motions of tongues, who could set out all the things whose number neither the densest stars of heaven nor the thirsty sand of the sea would match?

First, since the confused matter of things, which is called chaos, rose into the bright face of the world by the fashioning word, Enoch, most pleasing and beloved to God, having attained a living glory, passing beyond the measure of human nature through countless courses of years, fulfilled his duty to the earth by being born, but stirred up a marvel for death, from which he was withdrawn.

Sarah's limbs were already wasting, weak with old age, and her blood, extinguished by aged neglect, had condemned the veins of her aged body to the barrenness of despaired-of offspring, when, made fruitful by union with an older man, she suddenly swelled the lap of her cold womb, and, her breast swelling with a new birth, the trembling mother held to her breasts for milky drink a son, born with late happiness, for the hope of a future nation and people.

Him his father offered as a gift to God, whose promise had come in despair; the boy stood [with the knife] at his throat, and a ram became the burnt offering. O spotless mind of the holy priest! He rejected human things, he looked to divine; while he denied life to his son, he gained it. Abraham drew the sword to strike, and the Lord changed the sacrifice for himself so as to spare. A great mystery was surely being enacted in this piety: that for the life of the human race Christ, the gentle lamb, would offer himself willingly as a victim.

Lot was fleeing Sodom, which was to perish; his wife, by the boldness of a careless presumption, while she looked back at what she had escaped, was changed and remained a pillar of salt, not for wisdom, but for punishment. For no one who turns back with headlong desire to the dangers of the world once despised will enjoy the happiness of a pleasant salvation. Nor indeed is that ploughman worthy to rejoice in the coming fertility of the crops who, confusing the furrow of the ploughshare that should be fixed in a straight course by turning his face backward, has scattered the order of his past labour.

The bush, once wrapped in harmless fires, was seen to burn without burning; its matter neither supplied fuel to the flames, nor, seized by the fire of the heat poured round it, suffered the losses of burnt wood. So the touch of the divine kindling was tempered that, as the flame caressed the glowing branches, brightness, not punishment, was seen in the leaves.

The gentle, manageable nature of a rod was changed into an ungentle and unmanageable serpent: which, practising viper-like motions, as much bent in sinuous coils as darting its three-forked tongues, swallowed the twin snakes of the hostile deceit, and with a rigid change took on again its own form of a staff.

Through the depths lying hidden beneath the sea's waves, the waters rolled back to either side and held up by divine construction like a building of the sea, a crowd on foot passed over. The sea stood on every side like a wall, and the land, stripped of the covering of its kindred flood, remained bare, until the people, walking through the sea with the sea absent from their tracks, travelled a way of watery dryness, hostess to foreign waters. Nature changed its path, ordered to relax its constancy a little, and the countless multitude, crossing the plains of slippery salt, beheld without knowing it the raw mystery of baptism, having passed through the saving straits of the waters with Christ as leader. So, indeed, the prophet sang, signifying these things: "The voice of the Lord upon many waters." Who doubts, then, that the voice is called the Word? And who would deny that the Word of the Father is Christ? He, the founder of the old and new testament, laid open by his coming the immense abyss of the first law, so that by the more recent teaching, as though the masses of the waves were removed from the innermost depths, the following age, fearing no danger, might now advance secure along a path of level freedom.

Why should I tell how the countless throngs of that same people, in desert tracts of land condemned to barrenness of all food, obtained angelic food and the bread of heavenly grace, when a nectar-sweet cloud of the ethereal majesty, bedewing the people, poured out feasts from the rains and plentiful food from the showers?

Again, across fields parched by violent heat, the thirsting army was burning, where the land lay languishing, its springs denied by its ever-familiar heat, where the nature of water, failing, had taken away the hope of drinking and of living alike: when the numbness shut in the bowels of the astonished rock suddenly overflowed from the surging crag into foaming liquid, and the dry veins of the fasting marble spewed out abundant drink for all. In these three things, then, already proclaiming the great sacraments of his mystery, Christ was in the sea, Christ in the bread, Christ in the rock.
A she-ass, a cheap and stupid beast, terrified by the sight of an angelic power, addresses her rider in words, and the uncouth cry of a braying tongue unfolds itself in the speech of a human voice.

The sun at the topmost peak of the sky, reining in the swift course of its panting flame, stood fixed over against Gibeon and held the light fast through unaccustomed delays of the day, the evening being postponed; nor did the moon, moved by its own laws, cross the threshold of its sluggish station and practise the order of its usual step, until the sword of the victorious army, by the alliance of heavenly help, cut down the enemy's strength utterly. In short, the very stars, now serving, saw through the sacrament of a like name that the Lord Jesus would come, his name going before him.

Ravens, contrary to the ordering of nature, supported Elijah with daily meals, and the bird, given to the rapacity of a greedy beak, which supplies easy prey to its hollow throat, brought him food untouched with fasting bites. Now good and faithful to Elijah, the bird which once, bad and faithless to Noah, washed away on land the guilt contracted in the flood of waters. But he, being full of God, after he had shown many miracles on earth and, through the Spirit, as by a hereditary bounty, had passed the gift of his own power to a friend worthy to succeed him, was snatched up by fiery horses and chariots through those heights of clear calm, where the lighter way of a pure path keeps no furrows in the ethereal plain, since no track of the glowing wheel sinks in; and so he sought the more favoured regions of greater space that, shining on the axle of a heavenly triumph, relying on long life, he scorned the goal of the human boundary. How well, fittingly and deservedly alike, the majesty of the shining path smiled on Elijah's brightness, even in his name! For if in the Greek tongue one letter of it could be changed by accent, the sun might be seen to be expressly named.

To Hezekiah, a most just king, set at the farthest bounds of life, the Lord in his mercy, or by his right, added fifteen years for his safety, and, closing the threshold of death already thrown open, called back his life, languishing in its setting, to its rising source.

Jonah, thrown into the sea's waves by the panic of the anxious ship and hidden in the belly of the swallowing whale, did not feel the waters though set in the sea, having entered, that is, a life-giving tomb so as not to die; and, safe in the gentlest custody beneath the greedy belly, he was seen to be God's deposit, not prey, and, kept more healthfully by a hostile protection, he came to land by vomit, not by keel. In this deed, contrary by reversal, the sailor showed savagery, the wild beast provided the ship.

When, God inspiring them from heaven, the single purpose of heart of the three youths scorned and refused alike the sacred rites of Babylon, and accepted the harsh end of death by the cruelty of a tyrant's law, whose rage, kindled by the fire of Achaemenid fury, surpassed the scorching heat of his own furnace, the young men are thrust bound into the midst of the pyre, the pyre not daring to touch them; and they, burning only in heart, overcame the punishment of the image, the penalty failing. O how great is the salvation and glory of those who believe! The force of the furnace, quenched by the flames of a hotter faith, grew numb.

The author of so wicked a judgement, then, did not escape the punishment his deed deserved. For because, carried away by senseless madness, he had despised the laws of human kindness, he lived in the manner of a beast through the woods and, following the rustic company of cattle, exchanged the delicacies of the court banquet for grazing on hay and drinking from the river; and under this deformed appearance seven seasons saw him, shaggy, wandering through woods and mountains.

No less, later, while the fury of Darius, then reigning, imitates the madness of the past, Daniel, the most splendid glory of the Hebrews, is shut in with beasts goaded by hunger, and the harmless body of a simple soul is assigned to be devoured by savage bites. Yet the beast, made gentle and calm, so as not, though hungry, to tear the holy limbs with a mad tooth, began now to love its hunger; and rage, softened, lowering its terrible faces, and anger, resting more gently in the savage jaws, taught the lions then, forgetful of their native ferocity, to keep their prey safe.

Tell me, where after such things are your laws, O stubborn nature? Who so often took your rights away from you? Who ordered the underworld not to know a man carried off, granted a fruitful old age to a barren wife, compelled a beast to come of its own accord to the altar, turned a woman's form into an image of salt, showed branches glowing in flames not to burn, dissolved a staff into a snake, opened ways for walkers through the sea's waves, poured nectar-sweet manna from raining clouds, cast out waters from the dry bowels of a rock, allowed the mouth of a dumb beast to utter human words, held the elements suspended in a long halt with their courses fixed, fed a man by the service of birds and brought him to heaven on the axle of a flashing team, gave three lustres of life to a king already dying, granted a castaway to find harbour in the belly of a savage robber, bathed the limbs of the youths in the furnace with starry dew, made a wandering king a table-companion of wild beasts and cattle through thorny pastures, taught lions to spare their prey and not to love plunder? Surely to the founder of all things, by the contrivance of whose word all things, whether known or hidden, stand built, the foundations of his work lie subject; and the creation follows the command of him who orders, wherever the divine decree draws it by a nod.

Alas, wretched are those who, bowed down to empty cults, spend the foolish service of a perverse heart on images carved by themselves, and, abandoning their own maker, worship the likenesses made by their own hand! What madness is this? What so great insanity mocks their minds, that a man whole in his limbs should worship a foul bird, a most obscene cow, a twisted serpent, and a half-human dog?

Some, blinded in clouded minds, wish the sun to be reckoned the begetter of things, on the opinion that, flooding the tracts and spaces of the earth with the light of clear calm, it never ceases to traverse the regions of the sky and the stars with flaming speed: whereas from that very unstable motion, which the wandering fire practises in swift courses, it is clear rather that it is a servant, not a god; and, keeping the order of a fixed dispensation, it now rises, now, sinking towards its setting as the hours decline, shares its turns with the night. Nor is it always set everywhere, and it saw none of the first beginnings of the world being born, until, two days having already been completed without a sun, the provident Begetter had appointed it to shine from the beginning of the third light.
So also many pay superfluous vows to the moon, which they see always waxing and waning at the fixed times of the months.
So too they do not cease to sacrifice to the stars, which, at the departure of the driven-off night, are put to flight by the face of the morning light.

This one is a worshipper of waters, that one of flames, but they do not dare make neighbours of forms contrary to each other by nature, lest by nearer discord either the hotter fire dry up the weaker waters, or the pyre, unequal to the huge waves, suddenly die extinguished.

Another, setting up altars at the roots of trees and placing feasts before them, never ceases to pray tearfully to branches and trunks to guard his children, house, fields, marriage, servants and wealth. Wooden man, why do you beseech wood? You waste your effort shouting to the deaf; you await answers from the dumb, though you will hear nothing. These hold up the stability of houses only in this way: if, cut down with axes, they prop up the hanging roofs of the rooftops, or, put on the hearth and kindled, they serve in cooking feasts.

Some, more madly, are venerators of vegetables, and, watering their withering deities in gardens, show themselves to be true worshippers of transplanted gods. But it is shameful now to tell more of such things, lest, on a page of holy religion, while we rebuke the numerous errors of folly, either the rough bramble scorch the lilies, softest in their great beauty, or through the purple violet-beds of the flowering field the thistle and the Christ's-thorn armed with spiny prickles spring up. Therefore it is enough now, by way of rebuke, that we have laughed at the monsters worshipped by human errors, or rather have wept over such acts in pity. Now it is pleasing to go along the course of the path begun, to climb the lofty mountain with firm step, and with the zeal of all our strength to reach the city, the author of our freedom. It, indeed, is the house of tranquil peace, it the safe dwelling of salvation, it the everlasting lodging of freedom. For if, of the earthly city of a mortal kingdom, founded by a mortal builder, the poet of secular letters so sang: "And what so great cause had you of seeing Rome?" "Freedom...", how much more should we believe that the rights of everlasting freedom are in the city of the heavenly kingdoms, which God the Lord established as builder; of which the prophet of such songs says: "The Lord building Jerusalem"; and in the following psalm likewise he explained similarly: "Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem, praise your God, O Zion, for he has strengthened the bars of your gates. He has blessed your children in you, who has made your borders peace", and so on. Let us hear also the founder of all things himself in his Gospels, whose city he declared, with sacred speech, this to be: "I say to you," he says, "do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is the throne of God, nor by the earth, for it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King." As if he were saying "mine", which he refrained from expressing more openly, so that by humility of speech he might reveal the summit of his majesty. For so, when he was teaching, he admonished, saying: "Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart." Here is where the royal hall shines with golden domes, where he who asks receives, he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it is soon opened.
Here is that precious stone which, rejected by the builders, shines set at the head of the corner: whose burden is felt to be very light, whose yoke is proved to be most sweet.

So, through certain miracles of the Old Testament set out in order, we have related what the Father did with the Son as his partner and the Holy Spirit joined with him. Likewise, through certain miracles of the New Testament set out in order, we shall relate what the Son did with the Father as his partner and the Holy Spirit joined with him, so that the one power of the Godhead, always manifest in inseparable might, may be threefold in its single majesty and single in its threefold person. This is the true faith and firm belief.

This salvation the unhappy Arius scorned to hold. While he strove through the winding turns of a crooked, pathless track to turn aside the straight road, he slipped into the foul pit of murky Tartarus and followed the darkness; and as empty and void as he was of sense, so empty also in his belly at the hour of his just punishment, his entrails poured out, he breathed his last. Madman, who thought that the rights of the Father's divinity, which can be equalled by no example of likeness, could be compared with perishable ranks! For among men born by the law of the flesh, the son is less than the father, since the father himself, who now goes before the son, was a little while ago a son, and he who is now seen to be a son, no one doubts can become a father. So through the whole series of descendants new offspring run on, and the grandfathers of grandfathers are counted in vast old age. But the Lord Christ, who is the Word, the power, the wisdom and the whole common being of the Father, risen as light from light, was born alone from the alone; he is neither less than the Father in anything, nor is there anything by which he may grow, being higher than all things, since, begotten, not created, he bears for his supremacy the name Beginning: for so, according to John, when the Jews questioned him, he said that he was the beginning. What then is the beginning but the lofty summit above which nothing at all is found, abiding always in the Father, because the Father always abides in him; and the one head of all things, of undivided majesty, is God; not that the Son is believed to be who the Father is, but that the Son is believed to be what the Father is, as he himself said in the teaching of the Gospel: "I am in the Father and the Father in me." Then he added in sequence: "I and the Father are one." Let Arius hear that "one" is said; let Sabellius learn that "are" is said; the one fleeing from the Trinity, the other dissenting from the unity: both equal in error, though following different ways. Just so the authors of the pagan doctrines try to oppose one another with their sayings, who, thrusting out their arms bare from naked shoulders, are ready to hand down nothing by teaching but only to contend in long dispute, whose wisdom lies foolish, for the frail discipline of worldly wisdom is vain before God. This one talks more, that one is more silent; this one disputes while walking, that one pronounces while standing; one is always weeping, another never stops laughing: so in different ways an equal madness is seen in them all.

Meanwhile, as we lighten the burden of the toil of the journey with talk, and hope and faith together accompany my steps up the steep, we have come more pleasantly, the difficulty laid aside, to the top of the highest citadel. See, the hallowed banners of the cross now shine; see, the most holy camp of the great King displays a flashing light, and with starry breath the trumpet of the Lord's post cries out; the approach to his gate lies open to his soldiers: let him who serves as a soldier enter without fear. The door of eternity invites you, and that door is Christ, that is, the Father's voice. You will rejoice in the golden reward of everlasting life, you who manfully wield the heavenly arms of the Lord and, with the glory fixed on your brow, show the sacrament of the faithful sign. Behold, I, the least part of your army, good King, carry the consecrated glory and heavenly arms. Grant that I may receive a dwelling of my own here, and count me worthy of a small habitation within the walls of this city, so that, always your inhabitant and your home-born servant, set in a little corner of the holy mansion, I may deserve to be enrolled, last of all, as a burgess among the citizens of the blessed order on the white list of the page of life. Great things indeed I ask, but your greatness suffices to give great things, and he offends you more who conceives a doubtful hope of so great a mercy.

Christ, assent to my prayers, smile on my prayers, you who, hastening to bring the dying world to life, sought earthly things from heaven, deigning to take on human form, taking up what was another's but not leaving what was your own. Matthew, undertaking this, first set forth the man in general terms; Mark, like a wondrous lion, roared, crying out through the deserts; Luke, beginning with the priestly rite, took the likeness of the bullock; John, with the rush of a flying eagle, pierced heaven with the majesty of the Word. These four chiefs and heralds, singing of you with one voice, range like as many seasons through the widest expanse of the whole world. So too the twelvefold summit of apostolic height and honour, ever shining, imitates in number the hours and the months, so that, all things gathered together, the whole year may serve as your soldier. From here, then, recalling the old beginnings of the ancient death, I am glad to hasten to new life, so that we who sowed tears in Adam may reap joy in Christ, and may deserve to sing David's song: "Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds. But coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves."
BOOK TWO.

That most wicked serpent had driven the first-born man from the flowery seat of paradise by his deceitful arts, and by the allurements of a sweet taste had made him taste a hidden death, soon bitter. Nor had the violator of the command alone received, with the loss of life, the sentence of divine indignation, but the human race descending from him had been yielding to the condition of a long death. Alas, cruel and harmful wife! Or was that treacherous murderous dragon more so? He was the treacherous murderous dragon, but you too were a cruel and harmful wife. O grief! Only two had been immortal. Once the race began to grow, then it perished, and bringing forth disaster, it received ruin from its seed. What use was it in that age to have days many and manifold, what use in happy spans of life to pass nine hundred years and, as the tenth generation of descendants grew old, to see now blood foreign to one's own line, when the final lot of the human condition, seized by the last courses of the irreparable hour, though late, could in no way avoid destruction, and life, being short through a long age of time, lamented that nothing is lasting which is closed by an end?

Nor did any hope promise that a remedy for this evil would come, but the deathly desert of the first earth-born man would have swallowed with greedy jaws everywhere all the nations even of the last offspring, had not that merciful creator and founder of things, whose nature it is rather to pour forgiveness on offences than to threaten with punishment, deigned to raise up more firmly, through the same stone again, the structure of his work, weakened from its very foundation, so that the image which had been made living in the likeness of God should not be held unlike it through death; and had he not bestowed the gift of pardoning indulgence, and kept the children's teeth from being set on edge by the fruit which the parents had devoured unripe, and, most gentle and appeased, granted that from where sins had contracted death, from there boundless mercy should nourish life again; and as a sweet and most soft rose springs from a thorny stem, never to harm its mother, which it outshines with the grace of its loveliness: so from the stock of guilty Eve, Mary, coming with sacred light, the later virgin, washed away the pestilence of the first virgin, so that, since the former nature, stained by vices, had been subjected to the condition of hard death, when Christ was born through a human being, a human being too might be reborn through Christ, about to lay aside the foulness of the original stain by the renewal of the old body.

After the prophetic voice had often foretold these things, and the archangel Gabriel had announced them to Mary as now at hand, at once the conception of the faithful Word, breathed in, remained in the womb of the believing girl, and the heavenly offspring lay hidden under the law of birth, he who granted that all things be born at his nod. The virgin's bosom swelled, and the untouched body marvelled at the fruitfulness of its womb. The mystery of a woman's childbearing without a man promised great help to the world, when, darkened by the blemish of no stain, she nourished within her stretched belly the heart of her begetter, soon to be his mother.

Meanwhile the ninth month had run its course, and the light of the tenth shone immortal, and the promise of spiritual grace was made manifest in the virgin's offspring: "and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us", that is, he dwelt in man, whose flesh he deigned to clothe himself with. For the infant, small and very great, small in limbs, that is, supreme in Godhead, passing out through the pure chastity of the temple that hosted him, did not harm the body in leaving, which he had not harmed when he came. Truly this is the secret of divine generation: the birth is shown to be witness to the virgin, he who, entering as guardian of his mother's chastity, was both conceived and formed with the womb closed. What brightness of new light then filled the borders of the whole world! What joy in heaven! What radiance shone forth when Christ, with starry splendour, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, came forth from Mary's womb! His beauty seemed so to outshine with divine grace that the psalm of David declares of him: "Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, grace is poured upon your lips", and so on. And rightly it defined him as beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, because, although he took on the form of human incarnation and often called himself the Son of Man in the preaching of the Gospel, yet original sin had defiled us, which he did not have, who cleansed us by the purity of his birth. O mercy, gentle and ready to save! That the yoke of long servitude might not press upon us by the condition of sin, the Lord took on the limbs of a slave. Let us hear the voice of Paul the Apostle saying: "He emptied himself, taking the form of a slave", and so on; and he who clothes all things born from the beginning of the world allowed his limbs to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, and he for whom the bound of heaven is small, for whom the earth falls short, for whom the sea's wave is not enough, remained full in a child's body, God lying in a small manger.

Hail, best of parents, consecrated by the childbearing of so great a king, who rules the heavens above and the regions below so unceasingly that his rule, power and name know neither beginning nor end; you who, by the conspicuous honour of a blessed womb, are proved to be at once mother and virgin. No woman at all is found equal to you, who has either gone before your glory or will follow it in like manner: alone pleasing to Christ in a singular way, you are compared with no example.

Then, through the joy of the angel's words, shepherds keeping their flock in the night watches were the first to know that the Lord was born, so that the shepherd of the world might shine forth to shepherds, and the Lamb, newly born, might appear among the flocks. So, as the Gospel's words bear witness, declaring thus: "And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will." The faithful assertion of the Evangelist shows whose kingdom was in question here, when the multitude of the heavenly host praises God in Christ, so that, although the creation was human according to the condition of the mother, yet the one communion of the Godhead shows that the Father is known in the Son. They said, then: "Glory to God in the highest." Indeed the glory of God remained in the highest, from where Christ did not withdraw in coming. "And on earth peace to men of good will." We must believe that men are called earth, from which we were formed by the Lord's fashioning, who said, rebuking Adam: "For you are earth, and to earth you shall go." For then our earth won peace after that deadly war in which it fell, when Christ took on the earth of our flesh. For if we suppose that in this place earth means fields and mountains, what peace or battles can a mute and sluggish mass have? Upon men, then, that peace particularly came down whom it found capable of good will, so that wherever the searcher of reins and heart has seen the zeal of a sincere purpose, there he delights to set up the home of his dwelling. For it is peace, and the reasoning of a better choice, not to favour the struggle of the flesh against the spirit, but to keep both substances continually in harmonious purity under the dominion of the spirit. Nor ought we to distrust the weakness of the flesh so much that we seem to despair of heavenly help. For the almighty Lord Jesus Christ, who is shown to be the mediator of God and man, in order to take from us the excuse of bodily frailty, seeking only the zeal of our will, reserved the perfecting of the good work for his own majesty. For the apostolic teaching explains it thus, saying: "To will lies at hand for me, but to accomplish the good I do not find"; because, that is, to will the good is ours, to accomplish it is God's, who pours his peace into men of good will. Then the divine word continues, saying:

"When therefore Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judah, in the days of King Herod, behold, magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born king of the Jews? For we have seen his star in the east and have come to worship him. But when King Herod heard it, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. And gathering all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. And they said: In Bethlehem of Judah. For so it is written through the prophet: And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel. Then Herod, having secretly called the magi, learned from them the time of the star which had appeared to them. And sending them to Bethlehem he said: Go and inquire carefully about the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and worship him." Fittingly, in agreement with the ordinance of the Scriptures, the birth of Christ shone from the east, because it fulfils what the prayer of Zechariah indicates: "The dayspring from on high has visited us." For the psalm of David also contains something similar: "In the sun he has set his tabernacle", and so on. By the sun it signifies the east, the region from which the day always rises. Why then, Herod, do you rage so craftily? Why are you so madly insane? You profess Christ with your tongue, you persecute him with your heart, and you disguise under the calm of a cheerful face a foul mind condemned to the darkness of murky gloom. For you order Christ to be sought out, not to be worshipped with the devotion you feign, but to be slain by the deceits you contrive. You err greatly and are deceived, believing that he will succeed you who rules first on the royal throne, who neither succeeds nor departs at all, but eternal possesses the throne of his majesty; and you read the law and neglect it, you who threaten the King of kings over your kingdom. This guilt lacks words, this treachery lacks excuse: for you are trying to destroy him whom you had promised to worship. Perhaps you would have sinned less if you had asked nothing about Christ, so that, as a murderer only, persecuting him as an unknown man, you would not also seem a sacrilegious man who had offended God. Had you not read him warning thus in the song of David: "Do not touch my anointed ones, and do my prophets no harm"? Since, then, the divine command must be obeyed, so that neither his anointed ones nor his prophets suffer anything from malicious wickedness, because it is a great wrong that those consecrated with spiritual ointment should be treated with insult: what name shall this crime have, that you scheme by your tricks to have killed the Lord Christ himself, from whom the anointed ones are named, the true Prophet himself, from whom true prophecy comes down? Should you not have followed David, who served the commands of the Lord, who, when Saul had entered the cave in which he was hiding and he was being urged to kill him, [answered thus:] "Far be this from me altogether; may it not befall me from the Lord that I should do this thing to my lord, the anointed of my Lord, that I should lay my hand upon him, for he is the Lord's anointed." And he indeed spared an enemy who wished to destroy him; but you lie in wait for the Lord, who was born for the salvation of the world. And if, being forgetful of the ancients, you were moved by no examples, for this reason at least you ought to have laid down the weapons of your parricidal attempt, so as not to cast down the power of the sceptre you bore, you who are known as an anointed man persecuting the author of anointing. Yet, so that the bloody treachery of your name may not fall short of the full measure of so great a crime, what you, raging in vain, contrive, another Herod will later see, under the heavenly honour of the cross but the hellish crime of your nation.

The Gospel chapter, then, continuing, says thus: "When they had heard the king, they went away. And behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them, until it came and stood over where the child was. And seeing the star they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy, and entering the house they found the child with Mary his mother, and falling down they worshipped him, and opening their treasures they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh." What does it mean that the star which they had seen went before them, unless that, gazing on the guidance of a small star, they might find the source of full light? And they worshipped, because they had truly come to worship, which Herod, lying that he would do it, did not deserve to obtain. For it is not granted to worship God except to true worshippers, as our Lord himself spoke to the Samaritan woman, saying: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father too seeks such to worship him." Although, then, the words of the Lord's teaching are clear and open, that none but truth worships God, we ought nevertheless to examine more carefully the force of the saying, what is meant by "the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth." I think, therefore, according to the understanding which the Lord grants to my littleness, that by indicating the present time, in which he showed himself openly to the world, he said that the Father is worshipped in him. For so he made it plain in the following words, saying: "He has given all judgement to the Son, so that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father." And splendidly, after he said "in spirit", he added "and truth", since truth follows those who bear the Spirit of God, while deceit accompanies the one who is alien to it. Another mystery too is declared in the person of these magi: for through them, gentiles and strangers who came to him, our Lord Jesus Christ shows the grace of the law to come, that he has now prepared for all nations an approach to come to him. For so he is known to have spoken, both through his prophets and through himself. Through the prophets, though he foretold these things quite often, yet he set it out thus in the testimony of David: "The Lord said to me: You are my Son, today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession." He called the nations a wonderful inheritance, because it was being prepared to be acquired for the Lord through the grace of the New Testament. And through himself, in the Gospel, as the good shepherd, he promised thus: "And I have other sheep, which are not of this fold; and I must bring them too, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one fold and one shepherd." Nor let us believe that the devotion of the gifts lacked the divine will. For through those kinds, offered with good reason for their varied meaning, the power of Christ was openly declared. For let us inquire more carefully what the gold that was brought proclaims. Without doubt so splendid a substance, gleaming with the wealth of metallic brilliance, is recorded as brought to him as to a king. But in this king too we confess a twofold substance: for Christ both reigns spiritually in heaven and was born in the flesh king of the Jews. The gift of frankincense, because that incense once served for religious offering, is given to Christ as to God; and myrrh, because it is suited to bodies that are to be buried, is handed to one who was to die through the flesh, for the honour of a human burial. The very offering of a threefold quantity also proclaimed by its number the worship of the catholic doctrine, since almighty God, who beholds things present, past and future, and always remains, has remained continually and will remain, threefold in the power of his Godhead, laid the foundation of all things in the course of these times, although all things always stand present beneath his eyes, who has received neither the decline of old age nor the growth of youth, but who, being always what he is, does not cease to be the same. For when Moses anxiously asked the lofty name of his power, so that he might announce it to the people of Israel, he uttered this from the flame of the bush that did not burn: "I am who I am", and he said: "Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel: He who is has sent me to you." In the Gospel likewise, to the Jews who set Abraham above him in antiquity, he says thus: "Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am." See the difference between the two substances, distinguishing God and man. Of Abraham he said "before he came to be"; of himself he did not say "I was", but "I am", since it belongs to the Godhead to be, not to have been, for it stands always in living eternity, neither arises from beginnings nor is unfolded to ends. For time is from God, not God from time.

The text of the reading thus continues: "And having received an answer in their sleep that they should not return to Herod, they went back by another way into their own country." We too, therefore, ought to imitate the faithful deeds of the magi, and just as they believed a dream, let us now believe the most evident sights. Then we who, having found Christ by the light of the sign of the cross shining before us, have been found worthy to adore him and to offer him gifts of threefold praise from the treasures of our heart, will no longer return to the prince of this world, the deceiver who had earlier led us astray. Instead, leaving our former path, let us go on through the hidden tracks of him who directs the steps of those who trust in him toward the heavenly homeland.

Then the deeds are narrated in order as follows: "Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the magi, was angry, and sending [men] he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, according to the time which he had carefully learned from the magi." So, mocked by the magi whom he had thought to mock, the impious king made public in headlong anger the passions he had concealed. If indeed it is fitting to call him a king, who neither held to piety nor tempered his own passions by ruling them. Instead he was like a most savage and bloody lion: if perhaps a tender lamb can be taken from it, it turns its wild fury on the whole flock of little blood and devours, mangles, tears apart and destroys the softest cattle; the most wretched mothers stand far off, calling in vain on their young, already lost, and stir the empty air with repeated bleating. So Herod, goaded because Christ had been taken away, did not cease to crush the troops of little ones with bloody tyranny. For what crime, I ask, does an innocent crowd fall to death? Why do those who have scarcely just been born already deserve punishment? In the bloody king there is madness, not reason. Hostile to their first wailing cries and setting out to commit a countless wickedness, he slaughtered thousands of tender age, and with one grief bereaved so many mothers at once. One, pitiably tearing the hair poured down over her face, wounded her bared head with the disfigurement of lost locks. Another furrowed her cheeks, wet with showers of tears, with the violence of her nails. Another [beat] her breast bloody with hard blows. An unhappy mother, no longer a mother, falling upon the cold corpse of her only son, slain, poured out an abundance of milk with blood through the cut veins of her breasts. No one can set out the images of that calamity, so varied and so manifold, where the grief was not various, though the kinds of lament were. What feeling did you have, what was the purpose of your mind, no longer tyrant but butcher? What roars did you belch forth in your fury, when, looking down from the top of your citadel at the wounds of the innocent little ones, you saw a vast sea of tears gathered in flood? Yet among the slain infants, who certainly fell but did not perish, although Christ was away, he could not be absent. For he is always present in the dangers of his saints, and in his pity he himself feels the punishments inflicted on others' bodies for his sake.

And when, advancing now in age, he was twelve years old, a number whose measure he had drawn from the flesh, running, that is, through temporal age by human reckoning, he showed himself older than the elders in wisdom and a master to the masters in teaching, so that, as the manifest interpreter of his own law, though younger, he showed how great he was.

Nor was it after a long delay of time (what delay can there be in times, which flee on winged course and are already departing before they have come?) that, as the evangelist indicates, "Jesus himself was about thirty years old, being, as was supposed, the son of Joseph." Most excellently he kept both words, "about" and "was supposed", for the Godhead. For as he seemed to be about thirty years old, though he is eternal, so he was supposed the son of Joseph, though he was begotten of a virgin. Then he came to the streams of the Jordan to be baptised, seeking what he had come to give, to be washed who had come to wash. John the Baptist saw him. He had perceived him while hidden in his mother's womb, already aware of the Christ who was to come, and had exercised the office of prophecy though he could not speak. Now, coming down from silence for a time as from his mute father, he began to cry out and say: "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world." When he says "takes away", he shows that he does not have what he takes away. Indeed he took it, not in order to carry it himself but to destroy it. We see the rising of the shining day suddenly poured over the darkness of night's blindness, and yet the light does not lose the grace of its splendour by touching the gloom it dispels. So the Lord Jesus Christ, taking up the sins of the human race, did not keep them but put them to flight. For as fire makes metals bright by consuming their dross, so the good craftsman cleansed us from the original contagion with his flame. Then, stainless, he entered the waters and washed our filth in himself, having nothing of his own to wash. Lastly, purifying the very waters by the majesty of his sacred body, he blessed the fame of the stream, which attained the honour of the Lord's baptism. The waves felt the dread presence of the Godhead: the sea drew back from the shore, the river flowed back to its source. Of these the prophet sings, describing them thus: "The sea saw and fled, the Jordan was turned back. What [ails you], sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you were turned back?"

So the text of the Gospel reading continues thus: "And being baptised he came up at once from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, coming upon him. And behold, a voice from the heavens saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Let us consider more attentively how great a mystery is revealed in this place too. For after the Lord, baptised, came up from the water, at once the heavens were opened. How were they opened "at once", when heaven is never seen to be closed to Christ, whose home is always above the stars? But I think, so far as his kindness deigns to inspire my understanding, that the heavens were opened at the moment when the Lord, baptised, came up from the water so that he might mercifully teach by his example that the kingdom of the heavens is opened to man, whose likeness he took, when he has been found worthy to be steeped in the consecration of spiritual water. That the Spirit of God descended upon him in the form of a dove shows how great are his goodness, gentleness and simplicity, through a bird that has no bitterness of gall. And lest it be unknown that God had been seen bodily, it is affirmed by the voice of the Father saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased." This glorious affection of love contains the full firmness of catholic doctrine, and declares that there is one power of the Father and the Son. For love, which abides in God, does not depart from the spirit of likeness and equality. For he who said in the law of his commandment, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself", taught that there ought to be no difference between the lover and the beloved. And in the following word which he added, "in whom I am pleased", he is understood to have made clear the power of one Godhead held in common. For to have said "I am well pleased" is more than "I am pleased", because "I am well pleased" is a word of agreement and is seen to belong to two persons. The heavenly voice expressed it so that the Father might be seen to be well pleased in the Son and the Son in the Father. For in this very gathering together of the Father's voice, the Son's baptism and the Spirit flying down, the Trinity shone forth from one God. No one deserves to be found worthy of him who has not reckoned the unity.

"Then Jesus was led into the desert by the spirit, to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry. And the tempter came to him and said to him: If you are the Son of God, say that these stones become bread." So he was tempted by the devil, always the enemy of faith. For no one questions a matter that is plain to him except one who, full of deceitful cunning, does not believe the truth he has found out. Such is the devil himself, who learned from the clearness of the Father's word that Jesus was the Son of God, and dreaded the singular power of one who ate nothing for forty days and forty nights. (Moses likewise and Elijah endured a fast of as many days and nights, but he knew that they had done this upheld by another's help, although by their own merit, whereas he saw that Jesus worked by his own power.) Yet he suddenly seized on the emptiest hope of a foolish temptation, because the Lord was hungry. He did not dare to attack the Godhead, except that he saw the man mingled with it. At once, contriving his ancient snares of food, he roused his wicked tricks with his accustomed deceit, and pointing to stones, which are rather his own food, the serpent said: "If you are the Son of God, say that these stones become bread." As though he could not do this, who continually performs such a work: from the stony bowels of the earth he brings forth crops pregnant with fruitful food, and with nourishment growing from the rock in the dense ears of the harvest he bestows the rich food of bread from the fruitfulness of stones. But that singular wisdom preferred to disregard the glory of a wonderful deed, so as not to allow a repetition of the temptation. For God receives those who believe and shuts out those who tempt. For we read that the people of Israel offended God most of all because, forgetting his benefits, they dared to tempt him, asking in despair for food. Moses in his books was not silent about their unbelief, and David, recalling it, set it out briefly thus: "And they tempted God in their hearts, asking food for their souls. And they spoke ill of God and said: Can God prepare a table in the desert?" and so on. For what can be difficult for him who, because of his boundless power over all things, is called almighty? So the Lord, answering Satan, spoke thus: "It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God." A most apt and fitting reply was given to the enemy. For to him who asked whether he was the Son of God, he answered as a man, so that he might rather be defeated by the one whom he seemed to have attacked. Hearing this, broken and weakened, he still did not lay down the weapons of his boldness. "And the devil led him and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him: I will give you all this power and their glory, for they have been handed over to me, and I give them to whom I will. If you, then, will worship before me, all will be yours." What wonder if the wretch spoke perversely, who took the shape of a twisted serpent so as not to walk in straight ways, supposing that Christ would be touched by desire for a frail and falling kingdom, when he had come rather to bestow a strong and eternal one on his own? Or would he deign to acquire worldly riches, who had come to teach that they perish? Or would he worship a monster cast down from heaven, he whose throne is heaven, whose footstool is the earth, whose service is the whole world, on whom no one dares to look, and whom all the powers above the stars praise with lowered voices? But again the Lord confounds him with this reply, saying: "It is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." He is still seen to answer in the person of a man, disdaining, that is, to subdue the weak rebel by the might of his greater power. Yet that viperous malice, though thrown down in the encounter over this word too, did not yet lay aside its reckless temper; trusting in the flickering of its three-forked tongue, it raised its wounded head a third time against the victorious hand of the Trinity. "Then the devil took him into the holy city, and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him: If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written: He has commanded his angels concerning you, and in their hands they will bear you up[, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone]." Oh, how much blindness and gloom always rules in a black breast! A mind darkened by the shadows of its own malice does not know how to keep its deceit undetected. See: by saying "If you are the Son of God", he shows that he does not know it. When he goes on to say "He has commanded his angels concerning you", he confesses that this is he whom he sees. But by using speech with double meaning he is found out as both pretender and concealer, and is proved a liar by his own arts. A malicious heart is the home not of deceit alone but of folly too. For what more foolish thing could be found than that he should believe that one would dread a headlong leap from the high summit of the lofty temple and the top of the towering pinnacle, who came down from the highest citadel of the heavens to be seen on the level earth? Of him David cries out and says: "And he bowed the heavens and came down", at once holding the lowest things and not leaving the highest. So the divine voice struck down the boldness of the failing [enemy], saying: "It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God." Here, now revealing himself as Lord and God, he forbids the tempter to make such attempts any further. The kindly teacher warns us by his example that the spirit, the contriver of ancient malice, without doubt lies subject to human strength wherever God has been poured into the simplicity of a pure heart.

So the instruction of the reading says: "Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him." In this departure of the fleeing devil, and the angels' ministry that followed, it seems to me that [the Lord] declares by signs going before a certain image of the Paschal glory. For as the angels gave their ministry to the Saviour once the temptations were overcome and the devil driven off, so, when he had scorned the insults and punishments of the Jews by the blessed passion of the cross and had trampled down death itself, the devil's fruit, Christ rose from the underworld, was carried up to the stars, and with the accustomed sovereignty of his majesty is adored by the angels in heaven.

Then he called certain men from among the fishermen and joined them to himself as disciples, to fish thereafter for human souls. These souls, chasing the slippery pleasure of the world, had wandered on straying courses through voluptuous slips, as if swimming the uncertain paths of the heaving sea. And he won for eternal life men whom no noble lineage puffed up with birth of earthly rank, and whom no polish of learned eloquence lifted up with the glory of empty chatter; rather, men whom the holy rule of a simple life, conspicuous for a humility exceedingly proud, made already neighbours to heaven. For almighty God chose rather the foolish and weak things of the world, rejecting those that seem wise and strong, because, as the apostle Paul, the outstanding teacher, writes: "What is foolish of God is wiser than men, and what is weak of God is stronger than men." And at once he said again: "God chose the foolish things of this world to confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and God chose the base and contemptible things of the world, and the things that are not as though they were, to destroy the things that are." Moreover, the merciful Saviour, wishing to bring swift salvation, also laid down the manner and the words of praying. And the most loving judge wishes to be asked briefly, so that he may the sooner grant the suppliant's request. So he taught [us] to pray to the Father, his own by nature, ours by grace, bestowing his own honour on men, so that what he alone has as his distinction he might give to all as a gift.

"OUR FATHER, WHO ART IN HEAVEN." We who dare to call the everlasting ruler of the heavens by the name of father must first observe that the gift of so great a favour is granted not to individuals separately but to all in common. For though anyone, set apart from others and dwelling hidden in more secluded places, may implore the Lord in the words of this prayer, he will not say "My Father" but "Our Father", since this word belongs to Christ alone, whose Father God is in the proper sense. For although this is written in all the gospels, yet in that chapter the Lord Jesus himself clearly taught that the singular power of his right is distinct from mixture with the people, where he comforted the disciples, saying: "I go to my Father and your Father." In saying "my", he fittingly claimed this special glory for himself; in saying "your", he made plain that a general grace belongs in common to all. And since it is written, "Let earthly things teach you what heavenly things are", let us make some comparison here, so that from human things we may grasp divine ones. Let us suppose, then, some nobleman who has an only son and a number of servants. Surely, just because he is called father of the household, the servants and the son cannot stand on an equal footing of love with him, since the son himself is shown to be master of them all? We, then, use this prayer, not Christ, since by the words of this supplication we also call upon him, who with the Father is one coeternal Lord. So in saying "Our Father" we confess that we all are brothers in him. We must not scorn the affection of this name by driving out mutual love, nor follow the monuments of that original hatred by which Cain, who shed his brother's blood, became the beginner of the stain of kin-murder. Rather, glowing with the fire of a gentle spirit, let us lay aside the wickedness of the old flesh and rejoice to be clothed in the new man, lest, when our earthly works begin to fall away from heavenly ones, we seem unworthy of so great a Father, who, with Christ as our leader, has taken us up as his children by sacred adoption.

"HALLOWED BE THY NAME." What hallowing can be thought of by which the Lord, who hallows all things, may be hallowed, unless we prepare a pious, gentle, peaceful and chaste heart for his entry? So that, delighted with such a dwelling, he may work in us the increase of his hallowing; just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who always shone with the bright light of the Godhead, recalls that he was glorified in his disciples. For in the gospel according to John he prays to the Father for the disciples, and among the various words he spoke he says this: "And I am glorified in them", namely because he found his own glory in them. So where he finds the signs of his hallowing, there he says he is hallowed. For that goodness, gentle beyond measure, declares that whatever it brings to fruit for its servants is conferred on itself. A like sense is shown when he commands that he be blessed, though it is rather he who blesses all things. For the general hymn of the three young men singing in the furnace cries out that the Lord is to be blessed by every creature in turn.

"THY KINGDOM COME." We ask for the coming of the kingdom of the ruler who never ceases to reign, so that he may punish the deceitful prince of this world for his presumptuous tyranny, and he who alone is may alone display his own dominion, which knows nothing of death and cannot be consumed by time. For the day of that light, unbroken by night, knows no time; there the bravest soldier, having worshipped Christ and emerged victor after the various battles of the world, will rejoice in the crown of everlasting nobility that is to adorn the hair of his blessed head.

"THY WILL BE DONE, AS IN HEAVEN SO ON EARTH." Here too the sense seems to follow on from the preceding passage: that we ought to ask with unceasing prayers day and night that the will of him who wills wickedness to be nowhere may fill heaven and earth; so that he may not allow the devil, cast down from heaven, to harass the earth either, nor let the savage serpent attack the earthly substance of our body, formed as it were from clay, as food for his greed, and wrap us in most wicked persuasions, embracing and encircling us in his scaly coils, until, drenching us with deadly poisons, he consumes our wretched life by licking it away. Therefore let us constantly pray the Lord to guard in us both soul and flesh alike; for in one part we are of heaven, in the other we are reckoned seed of the earth.

"GIVE US THIS DAY OUR DAILY BREAD." For those asking for the nourishment of daily bread, a threefold sense of understanding opens up, though all the divine scriptures ought to be regarded so. So according to the letter we seem to ask specifically for bread from the grain crop for the sake of eating; and in the moral sense we pray to the Lord as servants, that we may deserve to obtain our daily ration; provided that we know the form of both explanations proceeds from spiritual teaching. For this reason we are commanded to ask for our food every day, lest by keeping anything back for the morrow we be seen to doubt the divine goodness. This, however, proves so laborious and hard that such a rule can be kept by few men, and very rare ones. For the Lord himself, faithful in all things, who governed the children of Israel, when he had led them out of Egypt, with daily fare for very many years in the barrenness of the desert, while they saved only the food for the sabbath, promised in the words of the gospel that he would give this to us too, if faith does not fail, addressing his disciples thus among the other things he taught: "Therefore do not be anxious for the morrow. For the morrow will be anxious for itself." But if we wish to understand more fully, in the spiritual sense, the words we are speaking of, we shall perceive that this bread is the divine word; if the mind is empty of its substantial teaching and remains even a little while fasting, it will suffer the want of great hunger. For there is no small difference between spiritual and bodily food. These we are commanded to eat sparingly, those never to refuse. Here abstinence is healthful, there greed becomes life-giving. Lastly, David proclaims in these words that blessedness belongs to one who practises meditation on the Lord's law day and night: "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence, but his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night." For this meditation satisfies and delights exceedingly, like the sweetness of thick honey, which, though it quickly fills the belly of the eater, is yet never found to cloy because of the nectar-like sweetness of its nature. Let us hear from this also what the same prophet says: "How sweet are your words to my throat, Lord, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!" He defined perfectly that the words of the law are to be understood as food, when he says they are sweet to the throat, not to the ears, and are served above honey and the honeycomb to the mouth, not to the hearing. For the deaf too, whom hearing does not help at all, are likewise filled with the heavenly precepts by reading through the service of the mouth. And the apostle, writing to the Corinthians, made plain that teaching is spiritual food, saying: "And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual but as carnal, as infants in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food. For you were not yet able." Who, I ask, would doubt or question that all this is spiritually figured? For not even a fool could think that they were infants or took the nourishment of milk from the apostle. But it befits us to know that those beginning to drink in the words of the law and to be gradually imbued with divine teachings drink milky first elements like infants; because just as good teaching is healthful food, so wicked teaching is harmful. Therefore the Lord warned the disciples to beware particularly of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, knowing that the poison of sour doctrine corrupts the richness of all sweetness with a slight touch, since, as the same apostle Paul says, "a little leaven corrupts the whole lump". For even if we believe rather that this bread is the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, it is nonetheless known by no means to depart from the spiritual sense, above all because such a feast and such a prayer is divinely handed down to none of the gentiles, none of the Jews, but to Christians alone.

"AND FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS, AS WE ALSO FORGIVE OUR DEBTORS." If we weigh the vows of our petition more carefully, we discern by our own examples whether forgiveness is to be granted to us or denied. For we are bidden to hope from the Lord for what we are seen to have forgiven our fellow servant, since the same pledge of equal terms binds us: that just as we do not wish to be debtors, so we should not desire to have [debtors] either. For in the persons of others we are either loosed or bound. But if it is thought uncertain which debtors are meant here, the material for a weak excuse must be laid aside: whether perhaps in a fault or in money or in anything whatever your brother is in your debt, release it. For both the frequent presumption of our offences and our dishonourable handling of sums of money show us to be wrapped in very many bonds before God. For whoever, as the measure of his means is weighed, is inhumane to the needy, denies on oath and disowns to God what is God's own, whose infinite mercy so protects the straits of the wretched that he testifies that whatever kindly stewardship bestows on a poor man has profited himself. In the vows also that we promise, having obtained divine benefits, we are debtors until we pay them with a faithful mind. What has been said of money debts, therefore, it befits us to understand also of the other and various kinds of sins by which we are held bound at the eternal judgement, knowing that a comparison from money has been applied to crimes for this reason: because the root of all evils is avarice, without whose vicious seed almost no crimes are begotten in the world. One commits murder to snatch from an innocent man what he coveted; another, solicited by a bribe received, becomes the sworn giver of lying testimony. It drives some to the pandering of adulterous traffic, a union of foul purchase; others stain themselves with theft, others deny a deposit. There are many other things like these, in which the ever-friendly hunger for gold serves as comrade. Yet no crime is easily committed which the service of money does not support. Therefore, having obtained the gift of divine mercy and attained the impunity of heavenly forgiveness, let us not deny one another what we have received, lest, having been loosed from greater things, when we do not release small ones, we be entangled again in the greatest bonds; and soon that merciful Lord, the giver and not the exactor of the debt, who released to us ten thousand talents, if he perceives that we are strangling a fellow servant over a hundred denarii, may order us handed over to savage torturers to exact everything, and, thrust into prison custody, we may not be allowed to come out at all until we pay back everything lost, down to the last farthing.

"AND LEAD US NOT INTO TEMPTATION." Not that the Lord, who is the way of light and the path of peace, leads anyone into the snares of temptation; but, recoiling from those who do not obey the divine warnings, when he abandons them, he allows them to enter. For all who, following the slippery contagions of the world and enclosed in nets of delights, strive after the luxuries of alluring perdition, are forsaken by the Lord, who is the lover of pure virtue, and go on to enter wherever voluptuous temptation has dragged them. Let us therefore strive to draw our foot back from it, treading rather the narrow path which, by a slender track unknown to many, secretly climbs to the steep gate of the heavenly kingdoms.

"BUT DELIVER US FROM EVIL." When we pray to be delivered from evil, we confess that he whom we ask to deliver us is good. And rightly the one who delivers is to be followed, the one who slaughters is to be fled. For in the one, through good fruits, is the tree of life; in the other, through bad fruits, is the root of the ancient transgression. For the Gospel reading has declared that deeds are to be understood as fruits, where the Lord, laying open the varied minds of different people, ordered each to be recognised by his fruits, that is, by his works, saying: "By their fruits you shall know them." Indeed, by as great a distance as heaven is separated from earth, fire from water, light from darkness, peace from war, and likewise life from the tomb, by so great a gulf of separation are good things set further apart from evil. For a twofold choice always serves the judgement of our deliberation, whether we keep to the right-hand path or the left, being neither ignorant nor doubtful that the right-hand path belongs to the just, rejoicing in the bosom of the patriarch Abraham, while the left is assigned to the deep punishments of the wicked, whence no one can cross over to the other through so great a chasm and the immense peril of the sheer mass. This, then, is the liberty to be desired by us: that if we are judged worthy to be the sheep and lambs of the supreme shepherd, we may deserve to escape the fierce bites of the wolf, and through the sweetest pastures of Christ, amid the most pleasing loveliness of abundant flowers, may enjoy a life now secure.
BOOK THREE.

The Lord, deigning to attend a wedding first, revealed proofs of his power, where as the chief guest, disclosing his divine might, he strove not to be fed but to have fed [others]. For wine ran short at the festivities, and amid the heaps of dishes gathered on the platters only cups already emptied lay sluggish in sheer dryness. Earthly drink had departed, so that heavenly drink might come in. So Christ then changed the waters, which passed over into the appearance of wine. The waters lost what they were born as, though they needed water for drinking, and the liquid, made nobler than it was begotten, changed its colour and its name alike. At last sweet new wine glowed red in all the cups, and through all the pleasant tables draughts of river-born nectar made drunk the guests, captivated by its sweetness. The servants of the springs were astonished that the six water jars which they had filled with water were darkened with overflowing wine and had all foamed with a sudden vintage of Christ, since he was present who is the vine, fruitful by the cultivation of power, nourishing under the shade of heavenly foliage clusters of the spiritual vine-shoot that will live for ever in delight.

Next a certain petty official tearfully begged the Lord to relieve the sick affliction of his dying son and to keep his feeble soul from slipping from the seat of his anguished body. Then the generous humanity of the divine power, which denies nothing to one who believes nor holds back its gift by delay, because it does not depart from the company of faith, granted the boy full health by a word and bestowed it by speech. For he answered thus: "Go, your son lives." How commanding is the Lord's power, and how magnificent, which did not promise that he would live, but declared that he already lived! For this is unique to divinity: that it sees as past whatever it has decreed shall come to be.

Then, directing his health-bringing steps through various cities and crossroads, through country districts, villages and forts, he healed every limb, driving out the ills of diseases; when suddenly from the midst of the gathering of the thronging crowd a leper, steeped in mottled misery and made more wretched by a loathsome whiteness, petitioned the Lord, saying thus: "Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me." No small faith was in this suppliant's word, who believed that the accomplishment of his cleansing rested only in the divine will. For as soon as the Lord touched him with his holy hand, saying, "I will; be cleansed," at once the two-coloured sickness departed, and, laying aside the horror of its spotted skin, his body was free of the alien foulness.
