He was seen by the people, changed by sudden help, and, now showing a healthy form, he seemed to be recognised more in his true appearance and less in his own colour.

A panting fever pressed hard on Peter's mother-in-law, violently afflicted, her inward parts seized by fire, and the torch of a powerful heat had settled fiercely in her burning marrow. The uncertain lot of her trembling soul hung between death and life, and the approach of chill death was being cooked by the excessive flame of her limbs. But when the Lord visited the sick woman, wrapped in dangers, with his health-bringing touch, the deadly blaze suddenly fled, quenched by a living spring, and the woman, rising restored and dutiful in diligent services, she who had just been languishing becomes the servant of her physician.

Moreover, in his mercy he often drove the madness of diabolical savagery out of the limbs of human beings who were dashed about, so that a spirit not divine might not rage when lodged in a work of divinity; and everywhere he restored to countless crowds the use of a wounded body, as the diseases fled, and rescued peoples from the varied ruin of sickness, as the danger failed.

Next, walking along the shores of a sandy path, he went aboard the planks of a small boat and, with the disciples accompanying him, had begun to cross over; and when the keel, driven by the movement of the swelling sail, was already being carried far from shore, a harsh and savage storm arises, stirring the whole sea from its depths with gales, and, when a wave withdrew and the stern was swamped, it lifted it again on the swelling waters. Despair of safety had troubled the sorrowing disciples, and even the sailors were forced to admit that no remedy at all lay in their skill; all, in short, believed that they were already perishing and that, either clinging to the timbers of the planks or rolled along by rowing with their arms, they would be dashed as castaways on rocky shores. But Christ, the true and provident helmsman, propped on a small pillow, rested asleep in the tossing stern, lulled in body, watchful in majesty, since according to David's prophecy: "He who keeps Israel will not slumber nor sleep." And when the disciples cried out together with one voice, "Lord, deliver us, we are perishing," he rises, roused, commands the winds to be still, orders the sea to be silent, and at once an unlooked-for calm of sea and sky alike becomes the betrayer of the divine presence. What, then, ought we to think of that storm? Did the sea raise savage gales against the Lord, or did the blasts attempt to stir up a rebellious struggle against their own Creator? Far be it that the elements attempted what would inflict insult on his majesty; rather, so that we may understand all things to be subject in humble devotion to the mighty works of Christ, the whole strait is believed to have been most joyful at the Lord's voyage, because it came obediently and running forward from the lowest seats of the waves, foaming with a whiter surge. So too the swift nature of the light winds, spreading its wings with flying delight, had encircled the stern where Christ sat, like the royal camp of a general, with a serving throng. For one whom the licence of violent power supports is not easily compelled to obey an imperious master, in the way that the sea and winds, bowing to Christ's divine commands, suddenly laid aside in languid torpor their courses, headlong in swift commotion.

Meanwhile the Lord, carried across the gentleness of the now quiet flood, left the boat and was walking along the edge of the nearby shore, when suddenly two most savage men, possessed by a grim legion of demons, leapt out from the burial monuments with a terrible roar, and were for this reason bound with iron links of chains. Alas, how heavy is the condition of madness! The one who endures the force of rending insanity must also be subjected to penal chains. Fittingly, however, that most wicked spirit dwelt rather among tombs and ashes, since it has nothing in common with life. Then, terrified at the Lord's coming and shut out from the seat of the cleansed mind, and fearing to ask leave to enter again into a human form, which it saw Christ bearing, it obtained leave, as its deserts merited, to go into a herd that delights most in the unclean foulness of filth and is always wrapped in the friendship of stinking mud. Indeed, being black, shaggy and bristling, it was eager to choose a dwelling like its own deformity; and at once the grim onset of the troop invaded the herd, drove it, and killed the swine as they plunged headlong into the waters of the sea. Not without reason is the devil called the enemy of all, since he is so harmful to everyone that he attacks those whom he hates and destroys those whom he loves.

From there the Lord, carried once more by the boat that served him, entered the borders of his native soil, where, because the Creator of all willed to be born, he called a town of that region his homeland. Then four men, with their necks set under a bed, brought to him a sick man, scarcely a man any longer, already a corpse. His life, lacking any movement of the body, was a prelude to the image of a funeral. Thus his limbs lay there, the bonds of his sinews loosened and let go, and through his slack and wounded joints, made foreign to him by the disease of withering decay, they could not perform their proper offices. When the Lord saw that he needed the restoration of his strength by heavenly power, he took care first to absolve him from his sins, which are the roots of all evils, so that health might enter the man, cleansed by driving out the squalor of filth, as into a house prepared for itself. So he says to the one who lay there, wretched then but soon to be happy: Rise, take up your bed and go into your house. Without delay he rises to obey the commands, strong instead of feeble, confident instead of despairing, about to live instead of dying; and taking up the little bed on which he had lain motionless, made drier than the very hardness of the dry wood, walking at last on his own soles, he rejoices to have done without the footsteps of others, and in a grateful mutual repayment of the favour he soon carried back on serving shoulders the one that had carried him.

While the Lord was doing these miracles, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, overtaken by the limits of life, had lost the last breaths of light, and lay a motionless body, now owed only to burial. Then her father, wounded by the disaster of his lost child, running out, he from whom the final end had taken away the already flowering hope of his line, weeping and groaning, rolled at the Lord's feet. Scarcely steadying his words of entreaty as sobs shook him, he said: Have pity on a bereaved father, have pity on an old man left destitute. I have, or rather I had, an only daughter, who, dying just now while not yet of marriageable years, is seen to have taken from me the name of father. Bring help and come to our aid, and restore the departed soul to the limbs already growing cold, you whom all power supplies, and whom nothing opposes in your power over all things. Scarcely had he finished such prayers, and already the Lord, thronged by disciples and crowds, was walking towards the funeral of the girl to raise her up.

Now there was going along, mingled with the crowds, a woman wounded for twelve years by an excessive flow of blood, who, giving much to physicians and gaining nothing, was being drained alike of her means and of her blood. But when a faithful confidence began to abound in the believing secret place of a heart already healed, she thrust herself vigorously into the midst of the crowds, desiring to touch at least the little edge of the Lord's garment, and hiding behind him, from the outer border of the hanging fringe she suddenly snatched a stolen health. O how much more it is, in obtaining hard things, to trust than to ask! For trust comes from the heart, prayers from the tongue; and prayers are often poured out without the heart, but trust is not born without the heart. See now: a woman, despairing under the torment of a long suffering, comes to the physician, not beseeching, not groaning, not lamenting, but in silence she carried off what she sought. Silence stood in her mute mouth, and her mind cried out to God. Soon a greater flood of faith dried up the streams of surging blood; and though all were unaware of the woman's favour, the gift of his own bounty did not escape Christ, from whose springs flowed what filled the hope of the trusting woman; and making public so faithful a theft, he rewarded the violence of the robbery with saving gifts.

Meanwhile they had come to the mourning roof of the pitiable house, where the untimely corpse of the maiden lay exposed to the tears of all, and a weeping throng and tumult had filled everything with the cries of bitter wailing. Flute-players were sounding, with modulated groaning, songs that flatter the dead below, and the joyless crowd, running about, clamorous with repeated grief, had thrown the unhappy house into confusion. The Lord forbids that she who was composed in sleep be wept for, forbids that she who would live be mourned as dead. For to all the body seemed lifeless; to Christ alone, who had come to bestow life, it appeared that sleep had been poured over her. And this indeed belonged to his singular glory, that he called the dead girl sleeping, so that, about to show the parents deeds of wonderful power, by declaring that he was giving less than he was giving, he might avoid the injury of human praise. Then, softening with the fire of the spirit the motionless corpse and the body already cold and bound by the stiffness of chill death, by the decision of his commanding voice he raised the maiden from Tartarus, and granted that a girl once born should live twice. The parents were stunned at their daughter, hesitating to believe what they saw, and moved by the joy of the sudden event, with tears poured out more abundantly in gladness, they changed the kind of their lamentation.

Departing from there, the work of restored light accomplished, he sees two men, wounded by the loss of their eyes, entreating with almost these words: Have pity on us, son of David. That mercy, namely, is what they were asking, that removing the darkening night he might restore day to their extinguished faces. How safe it is to believe, how sound it is to trust eagerly in God! For those already saw with the heart who perceived the path of light as Christ walked by. Then the eyes, closed by the sad blindness of the suppliants, like a sluggish fire when oil is poured in, flashed at the Lord's touch, and when his right hand of brightness was applied, the seeing faces shone with their own lamps.

These had scarcely been sent away when another weakling was brought, with a threefold disease, who, deprived of voice, emptied of hearing, his limbs empty since their uses had been snatched away, seemed full only of a demon. The Lord at once healed him, reversing the causes, in such a way that he emptied him by casting out the demon, and likewise filled him by pouring in voice and hearing.

Without delay he also hands over to the twelve disciples an equal measure of power, and bids them be able to accomplish all the things they see that he has done; and, rich in every power, he sends them to track down the lost sheep, namely of the house of Israel, because he had not yet spread the dignity of this name continually through all nations. Going, then, so he admonishes them among the other things he commanded, preach, saying: The kingdom of heaven has drawn near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons; freely you have received, freely give. It is as if the Lord, anxious with a shepherd's care, were saying: I, being the good shepherd, carefully entrust my flocks to you as skilful workers, and for their support in food I share out fields of my own right; so let no one sell to my lambs and sheep the pastures subject to my power. He handed this first to the apostolic discipline so that, propagated from their teaching thereafter, the doctrine of the following age might flow down to posterity, just as four rivers are read to burst forth from the one spring of paradise, and rivers without number, drawn off from their courses, wander through the bounds of the whole world. Whoever, therefore, performs the work of the Godhead, which he does not carry out as his own but has received as one worthy of a spiritual handing-on, having obtained the grace of a pure gift, let him be devoted to the grace of a pure gift, so that he may appear to be a steward rather than a merchant, and, fulfilling the song of David's joy, may thus declare for himself the hope of the life to come: Because I have not known trading, I will enter into the power of the Lord. For no one without the Lord's bounty can have what to minister or whence to distribute gifts, if he has not received what he pays out. Let us hear the apostle Paul saying the same: Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Here now it is required among stewards that one be found faithful. And again the same teacher warns and says: What do you have that you did not receive? But

if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? Then, when the Lord had entered the synagogue, he sees a feeble man, maimed by the numbness of a half-measured body, half-dead in his wounded limbs, wholly neither living nor dying, whose withered right hand the ice of sluggish numbness had cut off, already set aside, its use despaired of. Then, by a commanding and powerful aid, he granted that the hand, foreign to him with its failing sinews, should be brought to life into the warmth of blood by the movements of the veins, not by art but by commanding, saying: Stretch out your hand; and he stretched out his hand, and it was restored to him like the other. Truly this is God's singular gift, which he unceasingly exercises who takes nothing away from human health and always restores all things.

See, that slippery water-snake is here again, the harmful renewer of the tricks of his old arts, who, most abounding in the livid poison of gall, delights to grow fat on human gore; and the venom which he had often poured out through many people seized by various sufferings, he heaped all together, raging, into the limbs of one man, whose mind he snatched away, whose voice he shut off, whose light he extinguished, and binding together three disasters at once, he drove him, mute and blind, to madness. To him the merciful Saviour of the whole world, our light, the Word of the Father, after driving out the foul spirit, restored sight and changed his mouth; and through the Word words come forth, through the Light the eyes revive.

A woman too had come to be healed, bent more by an old disease than by old age, trembling in her bearing, panting with groans, curved in her shoulders, bowed in her face, and always looking down, stooped in her depression, at the lowly earth. Raised up by the Lord's mighty works after eighteen continuous years, her limbs held upright, she gazes on the sky and the stars, and remembers that once she saw the burning globe of the sun. You who worship idols, observe what difference there is between God, whom you flee, and the demon, whom you appease, if indeed he can be appeased who does not cease to harm. For all whom he possesses are oppressed; those whom Christ burdens with the yoke of most sweet lightness are lifted up.

Then, when he, as a typological Moses and a true prophet, saw that the people who had followed him into the desert were failing, overcome by the barrenness of the place, he restored the ancient comforts with increases most to be marvelled at. For then he made the sudden flesh of many birds abound, now the quantity of two fishes; then he poured out the richest manna from heaven, now, by distributing five loaves, he granted that a feast should abound for as many thousands of men. The number of the rest of the crowd went unrecorded, since the multitude of women and little children had no count. And, what you may marvel at still more, whoever you are who read these things through, if you have learned what was not yet known to you: after the hunger of the people had been driven out and they were filled, the mass of fragments taken up filled twelve baskets. Nor was the supply as great when it was given as it was in the leftovers, already disdained, when it was taken up.

Meanwhile, as the ocean received the falling day beneath the blue-dark heats of its surging wave, and pale evening announced the approaching coming of the starry night, while the master remained on land the disciples alone made for the sea in a boat, and the sea raged against the keel, exposed to contrary winds. Then, at about the fourth watch of the shadowy night, the Lord came walking over the waves he trod. With his calm step he pressed down the swelling billows of the foaming flood, and the sea licked Christ's holy footprints with a gentle wash. Those in peril marvel at the sudden new sight, that the ways for ships had opened beneath a path for feet. And while all were wavering whether it was truly the Lord who appeared, or whether uncertain phantoms of the darkness were deceiving eyes clouded by fear of danger, Peter, companion and friend of faith, whom a familiar grace allowed always to recognise Christ, asked that he might go to him. And when called, he went down into the sea without trembling, swallowed by no greed of the flowing wave, since, raised up by the help of the Lord's hand, he had fled for refuge to the safest harbour of the mighty right hand; and through the glassy plains of the salt marble he cut a path, becoming a wayfarer against the will of the sea. O the growth of increasing faith! Formerly he scorned the poor man's nets, the support of his life; now he renounced life itself, so that he might come to Christ.

So the Lord, having left the boat, trod the land of Gennesaret with the company of his disciples accompanying him; its inhabitants, welcoming his arrival gladly, gathered their own who were hindered by various sicknesses into the divine presence to be healed, so that at least by touching the fringe of his garment they might be cured of the harshest diseases. And whoever was found worthy to obtain this was soon made possessed of health. How precious this garment was! Or rather it had no price, since, sold in no trade, it itself redeemed all by the gifts of a small thread.

From here, as he was passing along the roads of the region of Tyre and Sidon, a Canaanite woman, anxious over the affliction of her daughter, whom a black spirit had occupied, besought him as a suppliant, asking to be made equal to the dogs, who shrewdly do not leave their masters' tables, so that, licking up the scraps shaken off, they may be fed on the scantiness of the falling crumbs. A most humble voice, but a lofty faith, which, once her daughter was healed, soon changed a dog into a sheep, and made one sprung up among the thorns of her own nation enter through the pastures of Hebrew grass.

Then, ascending the high ridges of a mountain, accompanied by a countless people, he restored to their former use thousands of the lame and the blind alike, gatherings of the deaf and of lepers too, and those weak in their hands, and whatever sick of the common crowd had flowed together; and he set the organs of the feeble limbs in balance with their own sinews and movements.

And while by the working of his marvellous power he revived the wounded host, the third day was running out, and in places fasting with arid dryness the weary people had touched no substance of food; and the languishing hunger was nourishing a trouble to be aroused by twofold labours, if the exhausted people, returning along the path on foot, should bear the long burden of want redoubling. Moved by this pity, the Almighty, who is always the bountiful bread of the needy and imparts food there where barren necessity has denied crops, by breaking a very few small fishes and seven loaves, filled four thousand men, besides an immense host of women and a swarm of little children comparable to bees. And, so that you may marvel at something more, the feast grew while it was being devoured, and fruitful losses at the tables begot food nourished by bites. Fugitive hunger was terrified at its own leftovers gathered in heaps of seven baskets, when, the abundance of such fragments collected, it saw a manifold harvest overflowing from a little seed.

But although Christ, from the event of his birth from his mother, was seen to bear the mortal limbs of a human body, yet he could not hide that he was God, because neither is a city set on the top of a mountain hidden, nor is a burning lamp placed under a hollow bushel, but, raised higher, the substance of the living flame supplies light to all. For having led three disciples with him as witnesses up onto the heights of the mountain, he was transfigured and showed the appearance of his glory, and his countenance shone like the fiery sun, his garments imitating the whiteness of snow. Why the most prudent evangelist compared the most splendid brightness of the divine majesty, which the keenness of no one's sight can behold, to the visible figure of the sun and snows, a clearer reason will teach. For there is nothing in this world brighter than the sun, nothing whiter than snow, and for this reason he judged that that likeness should be compared to the supreme Godhead, because nothing beyond this is shown to have been granted to mortal eyes. For that exceptional radiance of the Lord surpassed both the sun and the snows to such a degree that, while anyone's gaze easily suffices to look upon the sun and snows, the apostles, being unable to look at Christ shining with the brightness of his own light, fell with their faces prone to the earth. O great summit of sublime merits, to whom it was given to know in the world these things which the world did not deserve to perceive! What of the fact that they also recognised Elijah and Moses, unknown to bodily sight, with their inner eyes, while the truth of a greater faith, making itself known, showed him, the Alpha and Omega, that is, to be the beginning and the end? To him such prophets were seen to have come together, of whom the one still enjoys a living old age, and the goal of the other's final light no course of human lot surpasses; and by the oracle of a starry voice sent forth from heaven, when it says: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, the Father's voice taught that Christ was begotten by the Word.

But after the Lord resumed his bodily appearance and once more covered his heavenly form with the veil of flesh and showed himself openly to the peoples, suddenly a certain humble man, bowed on his knees, cast down with grief, entreating, prayed thus: I have one only son left, Lord, if he should be said to be left, hanging on the border between death and life, whom an unclean spirit overpowers exceedingly, and, tearing him, strives either to burn him in flames or often to drown him in grievous waters, and when he is worn out by many dangers plots his final end. Drive out the madness of his mind, I pray, and give him back to me, or to himself, so that the power hostile to light and blind may not take away the wretched boy's despaired-of life. He was still pouring out these words with tears and groaning, and the Lord with his holy heart was already healing the boy. Then the raging and turbulent robber, who had long harassed the ill-treated structure belonging to another, being about to move out of the dwelling of the house he had invaded, was goaded into burning anger, and, unable to tear apart the limbs he had seized because the Lord forbade it, he flew off into the underworld, the boy unharmed.

The King, too, who alone is King of kings and is shown to be Lord of lords, not disdaining to pay the tribute to Caesar, orders Peter, as he fished, to draw up from the sea's waves a swimming bearer of a golden didrachma. Then the swift dweller of the moving waves swallowed the quivering snare of the deceiving hook, and, hoisted from its native waters by the lashing rod, a most worthless fish carrying a rich payment, it was worth more by the honour of another's weight than of its own. How much, nonetheless, by this deed Christ wished us to be imitators of his teaching, who, though he could have refused the unworthy wrong of this payment (inasmuch as he had nothing in common with the people, except to help all with saving benefits), preferred to pay a superfluous due rather than deny anything to anyone who asked, so that the founder and teacher of justice, who said: Give to everyone who asks you, might be the first to fulfil the ordinances of his own law.

And when the apostles, simply as they used to, asked him who could be reckoned greater in the kingdom of heaven, as God and wondrous teacher he answered that the humble is superior to all, and that he surpasses all who has shown himself the last of all, like the little child whom he held set in the midst for the sake of a spiritual example, namely of small or tender age, instructing that the disposition, not the age, should be followed, since the years of infancy, of slight smallness, neither love anything of worldly pomp, nor are touched by ambition for honour, nor are puffed up by the swelling of proud disdain. And therefore the simplicity of a lowly life, the nearer it comes to the ground, the nearer it comes to heaven: for the mind that bends down is raised up, when raised up it is turned aside; and the lower course of the heart, by which it strives to descend, is exalted. For God raises the humble and poor from the dunghill and joins him to the company of the mighty; but the neck of diabolical pride he cast headlong from heavenly dignity into the depths of the filth of Tartarus. For thus the divine reading declares: God gives grace to the humble, but resists the proud. And again, recalling similarly, it says: Raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung, to set him with the princes of his people. For all poverty is the companion of humility. Hear Solomon saying: Poverty humbles a man. But we relate things far too small and slight, if, running through the deeds of the Godhead one by one, we go over them specially, which, though to be explained by no words, may become known in general.
BOOK FOUR.

Now when, crossing the streams of the Jordan again, he was passing along the road of Judaea, [there was] everywhere an immense crowd, and he cured countless throngs of every kind of sickness without name, receiving the sick and allowing them to return whole. Nothing, then, is difficult to grant for the highest God to those who hope in him, for whom the power is readily at hand to level what is steep and straighten what is crooked, that is, to bring the proud down to lowlier things and to show the path to those who stray. For the magnificent prophet Isaiah is known to have spoken thus, when he announced the coming of Christ: And the crooked, he says, shall become straight, and the rough places plain ways. Did he prophesy about rocks or thorns or the winding bends of roads, when Christ came to save a world set not in woods and mountains but in the human nations? This too is what the voice of one crying in the desert admonishes: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight, that is, the way of thoughts and the paths of wills, by which the Lord may walk with a straight entrance into the dwelling of a pure heart. For thoughts and wills are the ways of deeds, which are seen to precede anyone's good or evil action. Whatever, therefore, natural force denies is most easily subject to divine power.

For just as the huge beast, the camel, cannot pass through the tiny eye of a needle because of the bulk of so great a body, so the opulent and swollen rich man would be unable to enter the heavenly kingdom through the narrow gate of the strait path, had not the provident governor of things, who holds the whole by law and is not himself held under law, whom no face ever beholds, but who himself always watches over all things, consoled with such words the disciples who were troubled by this condition: With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible; for indeed not to all the rich is the patrimony of their wealth a burden, but [only to him] who is a bad manager of his own abundance. For when the Lord says through the prophet: The gold and the silver are mine, he shows that what is his is not evil, if a good worker has it; for it makes no difference whether someone spends nothing on good works or pours out a great deal on wicked ones. He indeed keeps his riches safe and lays them up, and hides and stores his treasures in heaven, where no bite of the devouring moth or the scabby rust consumes anything, nor is an opening dug through for thieves to steal, who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, hospitality to strangers, comforts the sorrowful in prison, cherishes those sick in body, and, most generous to all, is poor and needy only toward himself. Nor should one doubt that that substance will certainly reach heaven which is shown to have been spent on Christ under the most worthless guise of a poor man, which is increased by losses, is kept by being scattered, perishes so as to remain, and when dead brings back life.

Meanwhile, when the Lord, hemmed in by the accompanying people, had gone out of Jericho, he sees two men deprived of their eyes sitting on a bank, asking that their sight be restored to them. They made their request sitting, because hostile darkness resists trusting in the mobility of one's steps. Nor did that power, which refuses nothing to devotion and is accustomed to bring salvation where it feels faith burning, delay even a little; with a sudden waking touch it roused the eyes pressed shut by long sleep, and, unbarring the bolts of the windows hidden under the brow, as the day at once entered, it drove back the murky night.
Then, walking again about the sacred walls of the temple, he gave sight to the blind and restored walking to the lame.

After these memorials of noble mighty works, leaving the city of David, he had come to the region of Bethany, and returning on the following day he was making his way again to the houses of that city. [There was] a fig tree not far from the path, shady with interwoven coverings of leaves; when the Lord, hungry in the flesh, had found no fruit at all on its trunk, he wounds the inhuman branches of the tree not with a curse but condemns them with a command, rebuking it thus: May fruit never grow from you for ever. And at once the fig tree, widowed of its sap, which was withdrawn, immediately barren and unsightly, its glory of foliage laid aside, withered away. Yet let us not take these things literally, although they are believed to have been plainly fulfilled, since the divine law suits spiritual purposes. For what sin had matter without sense committed? Especially one that, as the evangelist Mark records, had no fruit by reason of the unsuitable season: unless the Lord did this for instruction for our benefit, who shows us the way of life by parables of deeds and words. Every effort of human conduct, therefore, which strives to nourish nothing that might please God, like a useless tree of sluggish trunk, full of leaf, not of shoot, will be counted equal to wood for burning, just as that fig tree too, standing fruitless, which the lord of the vineyard who had planted it ordered to be cut down, but left under a respite of one year, so that, if it yielded fruit even late, it might remain; otherwise it would then rightly perish. But indeed, according to the song of the psalm that says: The righteous will flourish like the palm, and like the cedar that is in Lebanon he will be multiplied.

Next there was brought to him a certain man who, along with the affliction of madness, also suffered the loss of speech; the breathing passages of his throat being closed, no voice sounded from the cymbals of his lips, and, uttering nothing at all with his mouth, he proclaimed by silence a mute insanity. But that starry Creator, accustomed to strengthen what is weak, shaking off from the siege of the throat the robber who pressed upon its gasping narrows, through the opened paths of the voice gave back to the tongue, released from its bonds, full exchange of speech with talkative freedom.

Moreover, while the Lord was ennobling by his own humility the banquet of a certain Pharisee who asked him, there came, having entered in haste, a sinful and notorious woman who, wounded by many wounds of offences, led an obscene life. And falling prostrate at the Lord's feet, she did not cease to wash his feet with weeping, to wipe them with her hair, and, kissing them, to bathe them with precious ointment, until the sentence of God, which does not regret giving a hand to the fallen if we now repent of the slipperiness of our old ruin, released pardon with such words, saying: Your faith has saved you: go in peace. O how much it helps the wretched sick to uncover by confession what becomes deadly when hidden! For he nourishes his own wounds who has concealed them and neglects to bare to the physician the sore lodged by the goad of pain. See now, a woman polluted by the contagion of a long disease is cleansed by the affliction of a little groaning, and washed in the flood of her own weeping, and, drenched with tears, wiped with her hair, she departs clean who had come defiled.

When the Lord had also come to the city named Capernaum and was teaching the peoples heavenly things in a very large assembly of the synagogue, suddenly, through the bodily ministry of a human voice, that most wicked devil roared out in such a cry: What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God. And soon, thoroughly terrified and cast down as the Lord said threateningly: Be silent and come out of the man, unclean spirit, bellowing with a great roar, by which he confessed himself lashed by the divine command, he left the human breast, fleeing unseen into the dark air. Likewise the Lord gave saving help to many who were sick in various ways and harassed by the calamity of various afflictions, and he did not allow the many demons driven out by the word of his power to speak at all, disdaining such a common witness to the faith of the heavenly majesty. For indeed that old serpent of Tartarus, the destroyer of life, the inventor of death, cast down from the heavenly summit with all the madness of his allied pomp and the whole foul retinue of his damned army, was astonished to see on earth, clothed in the humility of flesh, Christ, whom he had known as starry in that citadel, and he groaned the more, livid with envy, because he saw man so loved by the Lord of power.

And when, passing next through the region of Tyre, the Lord was walking on the shore of Sidon, he cured a certain man brought to him, most wretched with a double calamity, who, deprived of the functions of voice and ears, could neither give his own words nor receive those of others. But at the touch of the heavenly hand, all the inner chambers which violent ruin had closed being burst open, suddenly the doors, pushed, lay open, and with the guards of the veins at once loosened, he who just now seemed mute and deaf both himself was found worthy to speak and heard others speaking.
You too felt the gifts of the Lord's power, on whose eyes, pressed shut by the blindness of Tartarus, Christ spat, and on the spot wiped away the appearance

of a feigned death. And when, teaching the peoples by sacred ordinances to possess the support of everlasting life, he was revealing himself more plainly as God, avoiding for a little the crowds pouring in headlong, he came to a lake of sea-like waters, and, sitting in Simon's small boat, he had instructed with divine oracles the people remaining on the shore. And at last, ending his words, which were never abundant enough for their desires, he orders the fishing nets to be let down into the sea, the little boat going further out, nets which, though the course of a whole night had run its length, had been unable, their labour frustrated, to draw anything from the depths. Simon obeys, glad at the sacred command, and, skilled at enclosing the sea-roaming throngs with the siege of the line, he captures the peoples of the watery surface encircled as by a walled siege, and the multitude of fish so filled the stretched folds that both Simon's boat and the partner boat that stood near by, taken up with scaly masses, were scarcely snatched from danger. So too the unexpected happiness of a very great success often troubles us, and the joy which we receive as an answer to our prayers, if it goes beyond measure and limit, we now fear as an unbearable burden; because men are afraid to concede or even to wish for what is readily available to the Godhead.

Distinguished and renowned by such mighty works, the Lord, hemmed in by disciples and peoples, was hastening to enter the city called Nain, when suddenly he sees the corpse of a young man being carried out, raised up in sad service with the empty offerings of funeral rites, whose mother envious fortune had widowed earlier of her husband and now of her son, by the misery of a double urn. And compassion, enemy of grief, delaying not at all, at once lent life-giving help, and, having touched the bier with the hand of redemption, the Lord said to the dead man: Young man, I say to you, arise. And he who was dead sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother. For although the young man, deprived of light, had been overwhelmed by the torpor of sluggish death and was being borne as an extinguished corpse, neither could the servant keep silent when the Lord called him, nor could the spirit fail to return when Life was present. Soon, therefore, the whole gathering, which had been clouded with weeping, is restored with a cheerful face, and, setting aside its grief and turning its steps on the road back, a white-clad procession led the rejoicing mother back to her home.

Nor was it a slight salvation, Mary, that was bestowed on you by the Lord's healing: it cured the hidden recess of your breast, injured by many blows of wounds, [you] whom a sevenfold madness, massed in a demonic throng, possessed with seven movements of arms. But the serpent, spotted with a scaly splendour, fleeing the dreadful commands of the Almighty, driven out from your heart, sought the chaos of Tartarean hell, twisting the coils of its seven limbs and vanishing at once with its seven windings.

Then, so that the most fruitful growth of an abundant harvest should not languish for lack of the labour of few cultivators, he orders another seventy-two disciples as well, simple in mind, shining in purity, who, conspicuous in number and merit, would deserve to be called worth a golden pound, to go like innocent and gentle lambs to the harsh minds of men, as if among ravening wolves. He exhorts them with such words, addressing them: Go, behold, I send you as lambs among wolves. And again, when they returned eager because even the demons were subject to them, he said this in admonition: Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you. But nevertheless do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you; rejoice rather that your names are written in heaven. For this is the rule of divine judgement: to set life before deeds, not to put deeds before life. For if the merit of holy conduct ceases, miracles have no weight, since they are proved to be often displayed even by the wicked, to whom that witness of secrets and judge of deeds foretold in the words of the Gospel that he would say at the requital: I do not know you; depart from me, all you who work iniquity. Such were the two craftsmen of a wicked partnership who were once present under the Egyptian tyranny of Pharaoh, who, trusting in the vanities of Memphis, strove to rival the heavenly miracles of Moses, and set against them rival images and figures fashioned by magic tricks with human efforts.

Meanwhile, coming by invitation to the feast of a certain ruler of the Pharisees, hastening not so much for the sake of eating as to glorify his house, he saw a man distended with the swelling of a false fatness, whose belly, conspicuous with overflowing water, was thought to be a wineskin, not a womb, and the monstrous pregnant skin was in labour with an enclosed death, and the immoderate cavity grew with the wasting of the shrivelling limbs. Thus a leanness dominating everywhere had gathered the whole dropsy into the swollen belly. The Father of the world did not endure that this sight should remain in his presence, and paid no heed to his own Sabbath, which was then at hand, hastening to cure the man whom he desires rather to be his own. For God did not institute man for the sake of the Sabbath, as the Lord himself taught in his own words in another chapter of the holy Gospel, but brought forth the Sabbath for the sake of man. Then, imparting the work of salvation, he ordered the moist filth of the entrails to be dried up: when suddenly the diseased water of the bodily marsh departed, and the lake of the now glassy flesh, drained, is suddenly emptied by the departure of the watery plague.

And when the Lord, making for Jerusalem, was passing through Samaria and Galilee and Jericho, he graciously entered a certain village. As soon as ten wretched lepers saw him from afar, most foul with the spotted filthiness of their bodies, whom a many-coloured punishment scattered over their faces had made portents of shameful deformity, together with one voice they cried out tearfully: Jesus, master, have mercy on us. Then that singular power, which is never empty of compassion, answered mercifully and said: Go, show yourselves to the priests. And suddenly, while they hurry, all the affliction fled from their limbs, and, looking at one another, they rejoiced together at their mutual cleansing, because nothing of the horrible mottling remained in any of them. Of these one, as if to offer a tithe on behalf of all for the gift received, returning with grateful haste prostrated himself on his face before the Lord. Great was the man's faith and great his prudence, who in the effect of a single act paid the duty of a twofold devotion: faith, in that he believed himself cleansed by him whom he had asked; prudence, in that, though ordered to show himself to the priests, he preferred to worship Jesus. For who but the Lord Christ is the high priest of high priests, the priest of priests? The author and founder of the twofold offering, to whom, according to the order of Melchizedek, are offered the gifts of his own body and blood, which he offered for us when crucified: the sweet food of the wheat harvest and the lovely drink of the pleasant vine.

When the son of Timaeus, deprived of light, was sitting beside the road by which he had learned that Christ was passing, and, crying out repeatedly with a shout and not falling silent though the people forbade him, he asked more and more that the gift of clear sight be granted him, ordered to come to the Lord he went by another's hand, and, having gained his prayer, returned supported by no guide. O strength of unbroken confidence! How forcefully you obtain what you desire, and, gathering constant prayers from the heart, demand it as a debt; what you ask for you thus deserve! For whatever a harder matter, because of its difficult nature, refuses, frequent prayer of a suppliant alone obtains through simple and honest petitions; not that anything is difficult for God, but that the magnitude of the matter is humanly despaired of. Like that man who in the silence of night asked loaves from a friend who long refused him, and, because he could not win them by the right of love, wrested them out with the help of importunity.

The Lord too, passing through Samaritan territory, had gathered the heat of human thirst on a sweltering day, and the fountain ever living and always flowing with perennial water desired a little water to drink, by reason of the bodily substance he bore. Here a woman native to that region, who was drawing water from a deep well, while she hesitates to grant the gift of a little water, recognising by his prophetic voice the life of her own guilt with her numerous and alien husbands, begs the Lord to bestow on her such streams that, their supply never failing, thirst would fail, abolished; utterly ignorant and unaware that no one will obtain so great a gift except one who, immersed in the flood of Jesus Christ, has been satisfied with spiritual waters in soul, not in body.

And while the Saviour, thundering with the voice of the Father, was sitting within the walls of the holy temple, pitying the straying people and turning them to the right path with life's friendly admonition, behold, there was being led to him headlong, dragged by a gathering of a great multitude, a disgraced adulteress, to be crushed with blows of stones according to the ordinance of lawful custom. When the savage fury of the accusers thrust her upon the merciful judge, wishing her condemned, he set her free; for when the condition was laid down that he should be the executor of punishment for the crime who had no crime, no one was found pure by his own judgement to strike the impure woman. For no one dared to pull the speck out of another's eye when he knew the beam remained in his own. Soon, therefore, the whole fire of rabid sedition fled, quenched by the flood of conscience, and every accuser, by silently confessing, was found guilty. Then the merciful and gentle sentence of the Lord did not acquit the adulteress of manifest crime by judging her, but in pity did not punish her, she being, of course, to return to punishment if she returned to the fault. For whoever, in the filthiness of a dog's habit, seeks and licks up again what he has vomited, cares to keep neither the old pardon nor a future one, losing the gain of the one, which he acquired in vain, and feeling the loss of the other, which he did not deserve to attain.

The Lord, also departing from this region, sees a man blind from birth, who, slipping from his wretched mother's womb, himself more wretched, came into the light without light. Then that sower of the human beginning, the founder and perfecter of the world, not suffering the fabric of his work to remain less than complete with the material for seeing lacking, smearing clay, the natural instrument indeed, on the closed barriers of his eyes, the good craftsman supplied from the old cement what he had seen to be lacking in the man. Yet he did not receive sight until, admonished by the Lord's commands, he had come to the healthful water of Siloam, and, protected by the remedy of the kindred mud, had washed his eyes with the poured water. Soon, therefore, from the healthy face twin eyes shone, at last worthy to behold the day which at first they had held wholly unknown. All, therefore, who read these things spiritually ought to note what the mystic miracles of this deed teach. For we are a blind offspring, created from the brood of most wretched Eve, walking through the darkness of inborn gloom in long wanderings. But after God deigned to take the likeness of human flesh, saving earth was given us from the Virgin, which, washed in the fountains of holy baptism, opened the eyes of reborn clarity.

Then, solicitous, he had graciously come with saving steps to Bethany, where Lazarus, having met his end by the human condition, lay under a sepulchral stone already fetid in the course of the fourth day. When the Lord came to his tomb, the sisters gathered wept in pious mourning, the crowd standing by wept, and the Almighty himself wept with them, not in his Godhead but in his body, grieving, in that part in which he was to die, over the cold limbs of the lifeless man. For he spent tears as a friend; he showed the glory of his majesty as God. Why, Martha, do you still not believe? And you, Mary, why do you groan? You who hesitate in doubtful fear about Christ, whether he can raise one man from the underworld, who will make the countless throngs of the whole world rise again with renewed life. So when the Lord, by the wondrous command of his imperious voice, cried out: Lazarus, come forth, suddenly Tartarus, shaken with great fear, lay open, the inner chamber of hell trembled, deadly chaos was terrified, and the law of deep death departed; and the soul, poured again into the fibres of its body, the safeguard of the tomb broken, the corpse is seen standing alive. And after the due rites, after the burial of the funeral had been completed, as though he had been born and created anew, he himself, dying to himself, became one born after death, and went away a survivor of himself.

And so that the Lord, scorning the perishable things of worldly ambition, might show himself as God most high the more by humility, he did not make his way borne on lofty chariots, in which the love of mortal pomp is displayed, carried with the speed of a four-horse team while the wheel furrowed the dusty road. Nor did he press the high back of a snorting horse, which, conspicuous with trappings and purple, tosses its restless head, champing on the foaming weight of bloodied gold. Rather, the Lord found that honour enough: to be carried slowly by a most lowly little ass. Its hoof, great not in price but in the merit of so great a rider, shone the nobler under its burden. It was not unequal to that ancient one, which, though it saw Christ in a humble manger, yet knew him to be God. By his grace the beast of burden shone, and as it walked along the middle of the road all the people spread their garments beneath it. Tell now, all you peoples who until now lie under the errors of the gentiles: to what king was glory ever like this? Whom did a crowd ever come out to meet, thronging with palms and branches in full festivity, singing a song in heavenly hymns, except the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father governs the starry empire, eternal Prince in the Prince?
BOOK FIVE.

Amid these boundless riches of divine mighty works, the Passover had now begun to draw near, at which the glorious power of Christ was willing to lay down his mortal flesh, to take it up again, living now for ever, not another flesh but the same, which, filled with the reward of light, he raised from the underworld and lifted to the stars. And being a little troubled, fearing as a man the nearness of death, he cried out to the Father with such words in the confidence of holy devotion, showing himself the Son of God: Father, save me from this hour; but for this cause I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name. He spoke most divinely and powerfully, for when he was asking to be glorified himself, he indicated that the name of the Father was to be glorified. For God is his name, which Father and Son possess undivided, alike in common majesty. And a voice came from heaven: I have both glorified it and will glorify it again. What is plainer than the testimony of the Father's declaration thus fulfilled? What is clearer than the oracle of heavenly assertion? Yet the faithless Jewish nation, which had heard the weight of so great a truth, was in no way moved by signs so manifest to believe the Godhead of the Lord Jesus Christ proven. For some maintained that it had been the noise of thunder; others argued that an angel had spoken to him. O people truly blind in eyes and most hard in heart, of whom Isaiah, prophesying, spoke thus: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I heal them. For neither thunder nor an angel, a creature, begot Christ, its own maker, so as to answer him at once as a Father when he cried confidently to the Father; but a voice answering proceeded specially from the mouth of God the Father, who truly knew the Son, so that by this means at least the crowd, too unbelieving, might be pricked and led, though late, to heavenly faith. This, then, is the Father answering the Son: to sound in harmony with his own voice, since Christ, begotten by the Word, is the Word of the Father, and the matching correspondence of speech revealed the Father in the Son and revealed the Son in the Father.

Then, when in the sacrament of the yearly banquet he was celebrating the paschal feast according to custom, so that he might teach by his own example rather [than by words] that humility is to be loved, he rose and girded himself with a linen towel, and the Lord, the teacher, stooped to his disciples, washing his servants' feet, and laid aside so much of the height of his power that he did not exclude from the honour of this service even Judas, whom he knew to be the author of an unspeakable betrayal. But you were to gain no glory from this, accursed traitor, that you should seem clean in your feet, you who were defiled in your soul, like a tomb whitewashed outside, which within bristles, filled with the foul filth of corpses. Nor was the laid plot hidden from the Lord, but he marked him out as the head of the coming crime to whom he, the Bread himself, who was to be handed over to death, should hand the bread. Then the word of David was made manifest, saying: He who ate my bread has magnified his tripping against me.

But after the Lord Jesus Christ had consecrated the two gifts of life, his body and blood, and had offered spiritual food and drink to his own disciples, so that souls now faithful, fattened with heavenly feasting, can feel no hunger or thirst, soon the savagery of the foul spirit entered into the heart of Judas, a most wicked dwelling where it had found envy; and, seizing accursed weapons against the Lord, he stirred up the madness of a servile war, bargaining a great crime as a business deal for any amount of payment at all; for guilt does not lie in the price, but the crime grows strong in the deed. Blind, taking the small gift of thirty pieces of silver, he committed as much sacrilege as he would have perpetrated outrage if he had gained all the kingdoms of the earth together, the riches of the sea, and the whole region of the sky with its wandering clouds. For the goods of the whole world would not suffice to be compared with the shed blood of Christ, who is Father of the whole world, who allowed even this abominable man to be born. And would that, condemned by his mother's dry barrenness, he had not seen the day of his birth nor beheld the delights of heavenly light, remaining nothing in eternal torpor; and that lot would have been better for the wretch, not to know life given than to feel it taken away; or that, as soon as he was found fit to be begotten, he had been found fit also to die, and become an example of the first psalm, so that he might perish utterly from the whole world like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth, and the unhappy man had left no memory of his name. Then, therefore, bold, bloody, fierce, rebellious, mad; then false, cruel, unjust, venal and faithless; then traitor, robber, savage betrayer, merciless and impious, do you, as forerunner, guide and standard-bearer, accompany dreadful enemies, and, while you menacingly set in motion a sacrilegious host violently armed with swords and clubs, do you mar the bond with lying kisses, join honey to poisons, and fawn upon the Lord in a cruel betrayal? Why do you falsely profess yourself a companion and perform the greeting of a friendly fraud? Never does peace conspire with harmful swords, nor does the wolf offer savage kisses to the gentlest lamb.

So the holy worker of wonders, handed over to accursed men, did not abandon his customary help, but the ear of the servant, violently cut off, which Peter's sword had lopped, he at once restored and healed, lest at any time the merciful one should hold himself back from mercy. For it was not fitting that human vengeance should support God, who could have asked that more than twelve thousand legions of angels be sent to him for his defence by the Father, if he had preferred to exact punishment from the wicked rather than to forgive the wrong of his own slaughter.

So he then orders the edge of the bare blade to be put away in its guardian sheath, since he had clearly come to lay down his own life for all, not to take away anyone's. For to Peter himself, who then with confident voice had promised that he was willing to die with the Lord, he said: Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow today until you deny me three times; not accusing him of unfaithfulness, but disclosing the fear of the trembling to come.

Soon he was led to the house of Caiaphas, who at that time was indeed chief of the priests in the rite of the Jewish religion; but since he sat in the chair of pestilence and stood in the way of sinners, he seemed to hold the chieftaincy of crimes. For the council had begun to be violently inflamed and stirred up by false witnesses. A thousand lies flew against the Lord, dead in the empty embers of the accusers, not alive with the warmth of good faith, and all soon perished, exhausted by their own feeble motion, like a raging fire running through stubble of dry drought, to which the weak material does not supply strength to burn the high treetops, but the flame, at once turned to ash, loses its empty victory.

When no path smiled upon their tricks, fraud, yielding to force, turned to fury, and the impatient people armed themselves to raise their hands against the Lord. Alas for me, hindered by how great a dew of tears, wounded by how great groans of mind, I shudder to recall the sacrilegious hands raised against the Lord by the madness of rabid tumult! In short, the accursed people did not rest from striking his head with blows, spattering his face with spittle, and beating it with the slaps of their palms. Yet he, bearing all things patiently, gave himself up for our salvation and assigned his holy body to tortures for us. For through those blows we have the safety of our head; that spittle is the washing of our faces; by these slaps we have obtained everlasting freedom.

But the elder, to whom the Author of truth had foretold everything, since what Christ had declared would come could not remain undone, followed the Lord's footsteps as far as the house of the chief of the priests; three times he was recognised as being himself one of his disciples, three times he denied it. And the cock, herald of the day, crowed, and the oracle of the divine decree being fulfilled, his former senses also returned to Peter, who, recollecting the memory of his fault, rebuked in himself the error of forgetfulness; and as groaning followed at once, the sins fled, the offences departed, and the showers of tears poured out brought sweet pardon through most bitter weeping. Taught, therefore, by apostolic examples, we ought to discern the power and merit of penitence, so that, relying on such remedies, we may deserve to shut out deadly diseases from the weariness of our souls. For if we have been wounded by the harmful poisons of thoughts or of deeds, or even by the contagion of shameful words, let us strive at once to take refuge in the most healthful medicine of penitence, so that, grieving for our fault, we may not grieve from punishment, and weeping from the wound, we may not weep from death. Yet let us not prepare penitence for future errors, but apply it to past offences. For those who sin trusting in indulgence hardly obtain the pardon they desire, which many presume and promise themselves in security so that they may sin. For David too, a wonderful prophet, when he asked indulgence for a past error, in order to obtain it more easily, indicated by such a prayer that he had sinned through ignorance: The sins of my youth and of my ignorance do not remember, Lord. What then? Must whatever outrages youth has committed be kept for old age to be forgiven? Far be it that vices should remain and grow old in us. But since the divine clemency, with most gentle and patient long-suffering, has suspended the vengeance of judgement, let no hope of impunity dull us because of this truce; but like servants long runaway, let us at least return late to our Lord, asking pardon from him even as old men for a slippery youth; although it is fitting that every sinner at once, while the fault is still fresh, should cut out its ulcer with the knives of penitence, lest the first beginnings of a creeping disease, like the roots of a bitter shoot sunk deeper through the negligence of a careless farmer, can no longer be torn out entirely by any labour. Finally, the same prophet, lest he should seem to be negligently praying too late for the sins of his youth, added ignorance, so that he might more easily deserve to have his error forgiven by the merciful judge.

So the apostle Peter, too, did not set out to deny Christ, but fell simply and unknowingly into a lapse of forgetfulness. For he who had promised with full devotion that he was willing to die with the Lord could not bear to be seen as a stranger to his fellowship in the face of any danger at all. Among other things he had shown a splendid example of his faith: that not even fear of death could separate him from Christ, to whom, hurrying across the middle of the sea, he had once thrown himself into the rushing waves, deterred by no trembling at death close at hand.

Meanwhile the day that was to see a new outrage dawned, gloomier than the shadows of night, and, the murk of darkness removed, it laid open to the crowd the unspeakable counsels of the Hebrew assembly. Then Judas, the latest dragon and a murderer like the earlier poisoner (for as that one, by taking life away from Adam, so this one, by handing Christ over to death, became a persecutor of the human race), seeing the Lord led to the praetorium of Pilate, and bound in chains, he who loosens the chains of sins, the wretch went stiff and shuddered. Giving back the money, that is, the funeral fee for innocent blood, to the cruel stewards, and paying back the price of the crime, he emptied himself of it, not of the crime. For what can fear of death conceived there contribute to safety, where fear no longer brings any cure, according to the content of the psalm which says: There they trembled with fear where there was no fear? That is, at the judgement itself, where fruitless dread has no time or room for amendment. Or what confession can help one already placed in the jaws of hell, since we read: But in hell who will confess to you? For Judas, a public parricide, who, since he did not fear to dare it, cut the throat not only of his own parent but of the author of the whole world, sought the remedy of repentance in vain; the punishment of the sentence already held him after the boldness of the betrayal, so that the axe laid to the roots of the tree that had borne accursed fruit might, by cutting off utterly the useless shoot of an evil trunk, consign it to cruel fires. He was suddenly seized with mad fury, and nonetheless contrived a deadly end for himself, although he was saner then, when he took vengeance on himself for the outrage of the abominable conspiracy; and tightening, with his throat knotted, the passage of the accursed gullet by which the pitiless voice had come out selling the redeemer of all, he drove out his unhappy soul with a noose from a beam. A small punishment indeed it would seem for so great an outrage, which no magnitude of tortures could equal; yet the very kind of his deadly end, the death of a corpse hanging from on high, denies him sight of heaven and forbids him to touch the earth, so that the one guilty of an unheard-of crime, deserving to be expelled from both elements at once, might neither enjoy the air for life nor, as a man laid out in the common way of men, breathe out and give up his soul. This form of death also holds another sign of his own downfall. For the fact that the traitor and deserter met his death on a lofty height revealed from how great a summit he had fallen: lately a disciple, now a defendant; lately called an apostle, now an apostate.

When the Lord stood fearless before the governor's tribunal, like a gentle lamb led out to slaughter, the accusing people, finding nothing deserving death to charge him with, cried out in their zeal for sedition that he had called himself king, he who was manifestly present as king. Nor should anyone wonder if a people that loves deceit dragged the truth into a charge and rejected heavenly rule and divine power, a people that, ungrateful for the Creator's favours, once worshipped groves and served in obedience to idols. For it seems one and the same madness, an equal insanity, to have preferred Baal to the Lord then and to prefer Barabbas to Christ now; and while the righteous one is killed and the wicked one saved, a judgement erring in both cases changed the way of justice: the author of death was appointed to live, the author of life was appointed to die. From this, therefore, all of you who have remained unbelieving until now, believe at last that Christ suffered for the salvation of the world, who, his back furrowed by whips and harassed with insults, embraced all punishments, so that not even a robber, though worthy to perish for his deserts, should undergo destruction.

Alas, how grim is the edge of the sickle that cut down the harvest of the Jewish posterity! For those who, demanding the Lord's death, declared that his blood would remain on themselves and their children, saying and shouting in frenzy: His blood be upon us and upon our children, condemned all the fruit of their offspring, until this stain is washed from them spiritually by the water of him whose blood, sprinkled on them, rules in them to their death. Alas for the wickedness of your crime, Pilate, which you committed! You who in one judgement, or rather prejudgement, committed so many crimes, that if, needing healing, you had recognised them with a provident mind, you ought to have bathed not your hands alone but your whole body continually in the sacred washing of spiritual water. Unjustly you scourge the just one; as governor you put the king on trial; a mortal man, you do not tremble to set yourself above God. Therefore you are already held in the chains of a punishment to be paid, because through many wounds you nail to the cross the Lord of creation, and you fear to offend Caesar more than Caesar's maker.

And when Christ, handed over to military execution, lay under sentence of death, the sacraments of a great mystery were nonetheless enacted in the very dress which he received in mockery of a royal image. For his being clothed in the covering of a scarlet cloak showed the bloody look of his coming death. A crown of thorns surrounded his head, since he alone, in holy humility, bore the thorns of all the sins which had invaded the human race everywhere. He carried a reed placed in his hand, a sceptre truly like a worldly kingdom, which, because of its very frequent change, is seen to be fragile, empty, light and perishable.

And soon, stripped of the clothes not his own, he was at once dressed in his own, as if about to lay down in death the garment of the body, which he knew he would take back a little later, about to take on nothing changeable any longer, since after death he would return and rise again with the full majesty of his flesh.

Nor is it foreign to fellowship with divinity that he touched with his lips the wine mixed with bitter gall that was given him and spat it from his mouth. For it was a wonderful sign that the Lord tasted bitter death and at once scorned its horrible poison by turning away his face as he returned.

So, fixed on the high wood of the gallows, he changed the wrath of an accursed peril into holy religion; cruelty cast aside, peace mounted the cross; and, making illustrious with his limbs the violent instruments of the savage timber, he clothed the punishment with honour, dedicated the torture to salvation, and in his holiness, sanctifying the very torments in himself, made the sign set out for condemnation consecrated with blessedness. And so that no one may wander with an ignorant mind, unaware that the shape of the cross, which was worthy to carry the Lord and is to be adored, shows the reason for its veneration, everyone should gather by prudent reasoning that it is extended through the four regions of the world. For the axis of the East received the head of Christ, laid out with his limbs stretched on the cross; the western boundary smiled on his feet; the North shone with his right hand; the South gleamed with his left. And the whole substance of the world, made fruitful by the Creator's body, showed in itself the line of the cross fulfilled in its straight and cross boundaries, which it is seen to have attained from the beginning of the first light.

And when the soldiers divided his garments among themselves, they cast lots for who should have the tunic, since it had not been sewn but was woven throughout from the top, and they thought it wicked to violate the form of so great a marvel. Let the teachers of schism read this, surely, and know what impiety they practise in tearing apart catholic concord. For if it seemed harsh to sacrilegious and deadly soldiers to tear the garment of Christ, what an outrage do they commit who, disturbing the peace of the Church, do not cease to divide the Lord Christ himself by schisms!

The title too, written in a threefold expression of languages, in Hebrew, Greek and Latin letters: This is the king of the Jews, was read, placed above the Lord. It does not seem absurd to ask also what the meaning of this sacrament is. For nothing that is shown to have been done in Christ lacks a great mystery. Why then was this title read written in three languages, when the great book of the Acts of the Apostles testifies that many and various nations of peoples were by no means absent from Jerusalem, and either one language of an interpreter could have sufficed for the different peoples, or, if Pilate wished to set this before the eyes of all, he would have made it known to the common people instructed by the exchange of more languages? But since it was not accomplished by human arrangement, let us understand that it was fulfilled spiritually. For the true faith and the catholic confession, which was signified in Christ, taught that one king is set forth to the peoples in threefold speech; and that it proclaims him in words specifically king of the Jews, who rules over all creation, is fitting both to a worldly cause and to a divine reason. First, because Pilate, either from fear of Caesar or from the admission of his own belief, because he had called him king, defined whose king he was, lest by writing simply the name of kingship he should seem to declare him king in general and to proclaim him against Caesar, and to have become sacrilegious as if he had decreed death against his own ruler too. Next, because Christ is rightly named king of the Jews, and all the gentile world, occupied with the worship of idols, when it has been found worthy to receive the sacraments of Christian doctrine, will begin to call the Son of God [its king] among the sons of Abraham, to whom we read [God] promised that he would make him, as he also did, the father of all nations. Jesus, then, was called King of the Jews, not only of those present but also of those to come, because, leaving behind the useless roughness of their natural stock, they will soon be grafted into the olive by the ointment of the holy chrism, of fruitful sweetness, and will lose the bitterness of the barren wild olive.

What is more, the deadly and harmful mob, its spirit sated by no punishments, set bloody men on either side of the Lord, fastened under the same condemnation, so that the insult of such persons might heap up the blows of the wounds inflicted, although the likeness of the sentence did not have a likeness of desert. For while the just one hung between robbers and murderers, the punishment of the three seems equal, but the cause of the two is unequal. They indeed were guilty before the world for their crime; but before him the world itself is guilty, which was freed from sin by his blood. Yet the Lord, set on that gallows, did not lose the rights of his power: from the lofty balance of the cross, as from a royal throne, a just judge looking upon each and weighing the deserts of both in the scales of his divine heart, he chose this one and left that one, not examining the past deeds for which they were paying, but attending to the present differences of their minds. For one, from whom the savagery of his fierce way of life did not turn aside even in the peril of death, tore at the Lord with cruel insults and accursed biting words, like a shaggy goat, enemy to the shoot of the sweetest vine with the touch of its poisonous tooth, and spoke thus in mockery: 'If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.' But the other, more modest with a better hope, who, in sparing his tongue, also spared himself punishment, addressed the Lord with suppliant words, bending down to the earth his eyes, the only free things he had, since the stretched bonds of his wounds kept his palms, unwilling to be held back, from the office of humility. For after he had rebuked with a just reproach his companion, from whom he had now deserved to be parted, and had acknowledged the guilt of his own insolence, he prays to the Lord thus: 'Remember me when you come into your kingdom.' At once the holy Lord, like a shepherd gladly gathering again a sheep wandering through pathless wastes, addressed him, saying: 'Amen I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.' O wonderful and divine promise! He who was hastening to descend to the underworld says that he is entering paradise, so as to teach more clearly that there is no time in which God is not present everywhere. For, to empty the mind of the now blessed robber of the fear of death, he did not say only 'today you will be with me', lest he be thought to proclaim burial, but added 'in paradise', where an alluring loveliness smiles through the fields with everlasting flower, and delight, nourished by watering springs and gently poured through beautiful gardens, gladdens all with pleasing sweetness; and among the branches, blessed with leaves and no longer deceiving with any snares of fruit, that hellish serpent groans that the ancient dweller now lives without falling. So both, running with different motions, like robbers take the road of different paths and, bent on places far apart, committed violence distinguished by their deeds. The one entered the gates of hell, the other broke into those above; the one, sunk in deep darkness, penetrated the barriers of Gehenna, the other, entering the threshold of bright light, plundered the kingdom of heaven.

Meanwhile the whole world was suddenly darkened, overwhelmed by the shadows of a sudden blindness, and, steeped in a mournful mass of clouds, the day celebrated funeral rites; the sun, withdrawn with its rays hidden, veiled in a black mantle, lay hid and stained the world with the mourning of an alien night. For the elements, bereft of their father's comfort, deserved to take on such a face, so that they who rejoiced at his rising should grieve at his setting. For just as light shone when the Lord was born, so it departed when he died. Then a star shone by day; now it did not appear even at night. But although the light fled away from heaven and earth, it did not remain longer in this withdrawal; the very intervals of the suspended time seemed to accord with a great mystery. For just as for three hours the face of the world lay overwhelmed by darkness, so the burial of the tomb covered the Lord, shut in for three days.

Nor did the earth then stand without disaster, trembling in all its foundations as it perceived such things being done; and nature, thinking the end of the world had now come, hung at an uncertain limit, lest, that is, the highest summit, descending to the underworld, should at once drag the whole mass down with him into death, and the world, following its own Author, should flow headlong into chaos. But that boundless holiness of the Godhead was hastening mercifully to Tartarus in order to restore what was lost, not to destroy what was established.

And when those who had fixed the Lord to the wood of the cross saw such perils occurring, they were not at all terrified by so many signs, so many unheard-of portents of present fear. Rather, when he thirsted and asked for drink, one of the most wicked mob tied a sponge to a reed and held out vinegar to his mouth. O how fitting was that liquid to the most wicked mind of the Jews, who, having followed worse and lowest things, were called bastards, namely for the guilt of unbelief! For just as sweet wines, when they have been turned into sour vinegar, are rejected from all the cups of the table and thrown away, so this deadly and impious people, which in ancient times had pleased God, is now hateful and utterly to be cursed.

So when the Lord had fulfilled all things of his blessed passion, he himself at once willingly laid down his soul from his holy body, intending of his own will to take it up again himself, as he did, since he had indeed died but was living, dead in his perishing limbs, not in his divinity. Let us hear what John the evangelist reports in his person; for the Lord says to his disciples: 'For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul and I will take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself: I have power to lay it down and I have power to take it again. This command I received from the Father.' Who then could doubt, or would dare, that he who was free to lay down his soul when he wished could also take it up again when it pleased him, and work this power in himself rather than the one he deigned to show in very many? Behold, the gates of Tartarus are unbarred, thrown down at Christ's coming; the way back from the underworld now lies open; rocks are split, the earth is cleft, tombs are emptied of bodies, the throng of saints comes back to life; and, lest faith should fail in the believer, the multitude of those rising is recognised.

Then also that wondrous temple, full of ancient religion, seeing that the summit of a greater temple had fallen, like a sad and groaning foster-child mourning its own founder, at once tore its veil and showed its bare breast to all, signifying, that is, that the inner secrets were plainly to be opened to the nations and to the peoples who would faithfully come, since the law, which long remained covered under the veil of Moses, shone out when Christ came to us. Come, say, sad and impious death, where now is that deadly victory of yours, where now the accursed sting that served you at the tombs, you who, from the ruin of the first generation, never sated by any funerals, attacking the human race, are accustomed to lord it over wretched frailty with ever-punishing rule? See, now you, most wicked, have not come to Christ, but Christ of his own accord has descended to you, he who was free to die without death, who, begetting all things and establishing all things, did not create you alone, envious one. For venerable scripture says: 'God did not make death.'
