So if you wish to know the matter of your origin, you are conceived of the serpent as father and brought forth of guilt as mother; but now, as forgiveness reigns, you are consumed.

Meanwhile the Lord's spirit had now departed from the body for a time, and the cold limbs of Christ hung on the timber of the cross, and fury, still not abandoning its weapons, supplies a lance to a hostile hand, and with a wicked thrust violated the Lord's side with a deep-driven blow, opening a deep and dug-out wound, through which blood and water flowed together. O how this matter accords with catholic doctrine! O how these sacraments agree with faith in the Trinity! For the body, the blood and the water are the three gifts of our life. For all of us who give ourselves to Christ as our leader are reborn in the font of waters, and, receiving his body and blood, we eat and drink, so that we may be worthy to be the temple of the Holy Spirit. For the apostle Paul also speaks thus, saying: 'Do you not know that you are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in us?' Let us pray that the Lord may bid us keep this temple unstained, so that so great an indweller may make us, narrow and slight as we are, fit and spacious for himself.

So after that sacred place received the treasure of the precious body laid in it, the place which shone as noble while the Lord lay there and triumphed as nobler when he rose, the generation devoted to deceit, devising its usual wickedness in its impious heart, spreads it about that Christ would be carried off by his disciples stealing him in the silence of night, so that, as he himself had foretold, it might be published that he had risen after the third day. So the Jews, terrified by this suspicion of theft, ask that a very large guard be carefully set and that the gates and door of the tomb be walled with a very trusty siege. If you have not yet, you butchers, fulfilled your bloody office after the bitter torments of the cross, after the blows and wounds of iron, after the mortal burial of the body, and have not sated your unjust hatred after the death of the innocent, and do not rather acknowledge that the Lord of singular power, who so many times led souls out of the underworld, will call back his own: carry out the counsels fitted to you for the worse, nourish in your minds the deceits armed with the nourishment of treachery, seal the bars of the tomb, set military watches, shut the monument with a stone, and, furnishing everything with malicious arrangements, as you are doing, say: who will be able to guard God, to whom all things are opened and nothing is barred? He reigns in heaven, commands the seas, and rules even the underworld. Why then, disorderly mob, do you waste your work on watches and labour? Why do you strive to test a faith which you will not accept even when it is proved?

Meanwhile, after that sad sabbath, the festive day had begun to shine, which, most welcome to the Lord who rules, takes its name from his majesty, called by this honour the Lord's day, since it obtained so much dignity that it was the first worthy to behold the origin of the world being born and the power of Christ rising again. For thus the book of Genesis, the plain witness to things, says that on the seventh day, of the sabbaths, God rested from his works. It is therefore clearly evident that this day is the head of the world, from which, counting first in the fixed order, the seventh, of the sabbaths, is numbered; and the glory of the eternal king, making it illustrious also with the trophy of his resurrection, decreed that it should keep the primacy over all days granted to it together with religious honour.

At the conspicuous rising of this light the virgin mother, with the other women faithfully gathered, who had come together to the Lord's tomb bearing a gift of spices, furrowed their faces with tears and shook their breasts with groans. And soon they see that the place of burial lies open, empty now of the body, but overflowing, full of wondrous power. For an angel had come down from heaven and, the stone having been rolled away from the doors of the tomb, sat wondrous upon it, flaming in face, white in his garments, so that, shining with a twofold difference, he showed terror and joy together: terror indeed, threatening the guards with his fiery face; joy, comforting those who sought Christ with the delight of his snowy garment. So the women, strengthened by the angelic revelation, rejoice that the Lord has come back to life after death.

But the soldiers, terrified by such a sight, set in the balance of danger, can scarcely keep hold of life, and at once deserting their post they rush headlong back to the city, reporting the miracles, and freely announce what was manifest. After they sold their faith for a price, they are changed into cowardly deceit, and soon they invent that Christ's disciples, lying in wait with ambushes during the night's rest, snatched him away. Say, wicked and shameless guard, speak, criminal legion, what you mean to maintain, you who in your zeal for acquiring money do not see the pit of your fall and danger, and do not know how great a punishment you deserve, since you prefer to seem negligent rather than truthful. For it is agreed that you were wakeful, careful, sharp-sighted, that you never bent your eyes to sleep unless the next colleague duly took his turn to relieve the labour, that you so fortified the place with watches that it plainly could not be approached by any frauds. Was Christ, as you dare to compose with a false voice, carried off from the tomb by the hands of his own in the time of night's work while you were at rest, he whose linen cloths, whose wrappings lie there, around whose cast-off garments angelic power sits? Or did he who carried him off first strip and bare the blessed body, thinking it could be removed more quickly uncovered than taken away bound, as it was, though delay is the enemy of rapacious thefts, and it could have been carried off more safely and secretly with the Lord's own wrappings too? Iniquity has lied to itself. Yet this matter has the excellent grace of a figurative sense. For it is plain that Christ has been spiritually taken away from the Jews, whom we carry with the whole devotion of mind and heart. Lament, then, Judaea, your priests, lament your ministers and people, you who, deserted for such great crimes, will no longer rejoice in the trumpet, will not be strengthened by anointing, will not enjoy sacrifices. For in hope of whose power will the trumpet be blown for you, when you see your king slain? What anointed one will be given any more, when you have lost the rule of the Anointed himself? What victim will be struck, when the shepherd himself has been slaughtered as the victim? Let the synagogue depart, now darkened with its own colour: Christ has joined to himself a church beautiful with snowy grace.

This [church] presents the honour and glory of Mary, who, though she is seen always to be the mother of the Lord with evident splendour, is nonetheless always beheld a virgin. To her the Lord showed himself at once after the triumph of the resurrection, so that the holy and kindly mother, who was to spread abroad the testimony of so great a miracle, she who was the gateway of him being born when he came into the world, should also be the messenger of him leaving hell.

Soon afterwards he took part in a meal with certain men as if a passing traveller, and in the breaking of bread revealed himself to their senses and eyes, because, since he himself is the true bread, he becomes known to those eyes which inner faith, opening and uncovering them, leads by the brightness of grace to the recognition of the Lord.

Often too, at various times and moments, he showed himself plainly to the disciples: now appearing unexpectedly as they were eating, now taking food of roasted fish and honeycomb, so as to teach more evidently that the meals were matters of the body, by which, in eating, he proved to those who saw that he now bore those limbs which he had lately borne before.

Again, when the apostles, fearing to suffer the violent savagery of the people who had often denied the Lord, stayed behind the closed doors of a house, he, standing unexpectedly at the barred doors, gave peace to all in the greeting of his speech, so that, granting joy in recompense to the afflicted, he might confirm what he had signified by the prophetic voice, that the Lord will not abandon a contrite and humbled heart. And soon he opened his pierced hands and bared the wound driven into his side, so that they should not think him a phantom if they did not see the marks of the wounds.

But since Thomas, an equally venerable apostle, whom they called by the name Didymus, was not present there, and did not believe when his companions reported such things: see, the Lord afterwards, when he was sitting with the brothers, presents himself again with the doors unmoved, he who had never departed from them spiritually, and, seen before all in their midst, does not disdain to humour the trembling disciple: and, showing again his palms and side, allows himself to be proved by the touch of his wounds, recognised the more from this as being himself the Christ, because he received and cherished the doubter's mind with calm gentleness. For whoever practises crafty deceits under the blind image of fraud and contrives empty mists and shapes to deceive unwary minds does not wish to be examined, does not wish his deeds to be known, so that he may lie hidden under the veil of a deceitful cloud, and, mocking wretched eyes with contrived phantoms, he hates the careful, if he begins to be found out, even his friends. But Christ the Lord, truthful in all things, most gentle even toward one doubting to believe, is not angry with the hesitant, but with mild readiness allows him even to plunge his fingers into the wounds, knowing that the example of this proof concerns not only Thomas, who was already blessed, but the faith of many thereafter.

After a few days the Lord again showed himself on the sea-shore to Peter as he was fishing with his companions, and, seeing that they were weary and had made no catch in the wakeful labour of the whole night, he orders the nets to be let down on the right into the sea, and at once, the brine of the deep enclosed, the bulging folds brought up an immense gathering of fish with the catch, which they joyfully threw down before the Lord's feet. Such a kind of miracle, then, ought not to be taken as an ordinary deed, but weighed with figurative understanding. For let us believe the nets to be the commandments of God, exceedingly bright and clear, in which all who follow the right, to be rescued from the waves of the world, are enclosed, bowed at the feet of Christ.

For the fish too, laid upon the coals, and the bread found by them at the same time in the same place, is seen not to lack catholic meaning. For the fish seems to be understood as the water in which it is certain we are washed and reborn; the bread signifies Christ the Saviour, by whose same body we are fed unto salvation. The fire bears the image of the Holy Spirit, by whom we are devoutly consecrated to faith. For he shone forth shown in this same form when he flooded the blessed apostles with his bright divinity, as the book of their Acts testifies. Then he invites them to take food with the calm command of solemn words, and they, soon gathered with one mind at the Lord's table, receive the food of holy blessing and recognise Christ in the full truth of faith.

When they had risen, suitably filled with the modest meal, the Lord gently asks him whether he loves him. And to him, at once assenting, he, wishing as a good shepherd to increase his flocks, entrusts his sheep and lambs, as to a most faithful and approved worker. And this he repeats and goes over a third time, so that the threefold denial of the recent fault might be cleansed by an equal number of [professions of] love. But that he gave Peter in particular the dignity of feeding the flock, though he is shown to love all equally, does not tend to the detriment of the others, but seems joined to reason. For this most gentle animal, for the simplicity of its nature, is compared to the just, whom, when the king of all comes in his majesty, he will address in this way as they stand at his right, as he himself taught: 'Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,' and so on. Fittingly, then, he entrusts the just who are to enter the kingdom to him to whom he had promised to give the keys of that same kingdom.

Then, instructing them with blessed counsels and strengthening them with the handing on of peaceful teaching, he commands them to spread the precepts of religious faith through all lands and to bestow on all nations the single Trinity of holy baptism, saying and decreeing thus: 'All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go now and teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things whatsoever I have commanded you,' and so on.

And when he had ordered all things of divinity to be fulfilled, soon, having gone out to Bethany with the same men led out together, straightway before the blessed men who were worthy to obtain the sight of so great a triumph, carried up through the regions of the upper air, he ascends the citadel of starry dominion and sits at the right hand of the Father's majesty, and rules and governs all things by his own will, he who, ever possessing all things high and deep, after heaven descended to Tartarus, and after Tartarus returned to heaven. For this reason, then, he wished to pass to the stars with these same men present (as far as he deigns to open it to the senses of my littleness), so that he might show them the way by which they should follow, to whom, when they said to him before the passion, 'Lord, we do not know where you are going; how can we know the way?', he answered plainly and said: 'I am the way and the truth and the life.' The way, since through him one comes to the grace of the Father. The truth, because he grants to believers what he promises. The life, since those whom he adopts are not subject to death. So the disciples, most joyful, beholding the Lord high above the clouds, treading with his own feet the gleaming tracts of the stars, the world conquered, humbly venerate and adore him, and in a most welcome return they turn over in their hearts and carry back the regions of the airy path that served his steps, which they had seen with their eyes, to admonish all nations to believe. For they are proved to be faithful and very great witnesses of divine power, who, seeing the innumerable deeds of the Lord Jesus Christ, wrote down a few of his noble acts. For if all the miracles of our Saviour could have been bound into religious pages, perhaps not even the world itself, as John the evangelist testifies, could contain all the volumes of books that would be written.
